📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BYD opened pre-orders for the third-generation Tang starting at about $34,000 in China. This five-seat flagship SUV packs more than you’d expect for the money, with two massive 30-inch-plus screens inside and up to 850 km (528 miles) of CLTC range.

The third-generation Tang joins the Great Tang, or Da Tang, as it’s called in China in BYD’s expanding flagship SUV lineup.

We knew it was coming soon after the upcoming model appeared in a regulatory filing in China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) last month.

BYD announced on Friday that pre-orders for the third-gen Tang are officially open, starting at 225,000 yuan, which is around $34,000.

The “large five-seat flagship SUV,” as BYD calls it, is available in three variants, priced from 225,000 yuan ($34,000), 240,000 yuan ($36,000), and 260,000 yuan ($39,000) with rear- and all-wheel-drive variants.

The two lower-priced variants are both RWD, offering a CLTC range of up to 850 km (528 miles), while the top-spec dual-motor AWD version has up to 770 km (478 miles).

All versions use BYD’s second-generation Blade Batteries and Flash Charging tech, enabling the battery to be charged from 10% to 80% in five minutes, or nine minutes to go from 10% to 97%.

Inside, the five-seat SUV packs a surprising amount of tech and premium extras for the price. The setup features two massive screens: a 35.4″ integrated display and another 30″ panoramic theater screen.

Unlike its predessor, which offered five and six-seat configurations, the third-gen Tang will only be offered as a five-seater.

The five-seat setup opens up interior space for passengers and the third-gen Tang has the largest front trunk (frunk) in its class at 205L, BYD said.

Like many of its new flagship vehicles, the third-gen Tang is equipped with BYD’s latest tech, including its God’s Eye B driver-assistance system and Disus-A dual-chamber intelligent air suspension body control system.

Other added features include a 22-speaker Dynaudio sound system, intelligent electric all‑wheel drive, a high-speed tire blowout stability system, and its iTAC intelligent torque control system.

Lu Tian, the general manager of BYD’s Dynasty division said third-gen Tang vehicles have arrived at dealerships nationwide.

Industry observers note that why mention "two enormous screens" like they are some markers of a more premium vehicle or represent some value? We don't measure the utility of cars by screen real estate per dollar. It's the other part of the utility that matter: range, driving dynamics, road trip convenience, fit/finish/materials/insulation. Personally, I don't think "enormous screens" are going to age well as an automotive trend.

The Great Tang received over 150,000 preorders by the time it launched in mid-June, a record for a single BYD model.

Since its official launch, the larger Great Tang (Da Tang) has sold more than 10,000 units for four straight months now.

The Great Tang is on sale in China in pure electric (EV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrains. The cheapest EV variant starts at 239,900 yuan ($35,500) a CLTC driving range of 800 km (497 miles). Starting at just 269,900 yuan ($40,000), the Flagship EV version uses a bigger (130.15 kWh) battery, offering a CLTC range of up to 590 miles (950 km).

In a recent development, will BYD’s smaller five-seat SUV draw the same demand? Let us know your thoughts in the comments below.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that stories about Flock cameras and other stalkerish automatic license plate readers (ALPRs) have been a mainstay of American news for the last year or two, and horror stories involving this questionable technology are everywhere. From police using ALPRs to stalk citizens to AI-powered ALPRs flagging innocent auto journalists for stealing vehicles, there's no shortage of evidence that ALPRs are making the world worse. A lot of such stories you see in the news and even here on Jalopnik are about misuse of and problems with ALPRs specifically in the United States, though. While there's certainly some bias toward American news on publications based in the States, it still does raise the question: Are there Flock cameras or equivalents in other countries? And if so, do they cause the same volume of issues?

Recent findings suggest that the answer is an interesting one. First, yes, ALPRs do exist outside of the United States, though the technology is often called automatic number plate recognition, or ANPR, due to regional differences in how license plates are referred to. Nearly 100 countries use this technology to track automobile movement and other data. However, Flock cameras themselves aren't nearly as prevalent outside the United States. In fact, the big difference between the implementation of license plate recognition technology in the U.S. and abroad is in who owns it and how the data collected is managed.

See, Flock Safety and Axon, two of the biggest promulgators of ALPR tech in the States, are privately operated companies that contract their services out to the state via entities like police departments and city councils. In other countries, and European countries in particular, ALPRs are typically owned, deployed, and operated by the state itself, rather than subcontracted through private companies. This distinction might just make all the difference.

If you're skeptical that a state-owned surveillance network is different than a privately owned, state-sponsored surveillance, well, you know, that's fair. But there are indeed some notable differences between how this technology is treated in the U.S. and how it's used abroad.

The rest of the world is certainly no stranger to surveillance. For example, the UK has a massive network of CCTV cameras that leave urban areas like London heavily monitored at all times, and they're now employing AI to level up their surveillance efforts, too. AI-powered surveillance is also rapidly ramping up in China, Brazil, and Australia.

Recent findings suggest that whether these networks are installed and operated by governments or private entities, the fact is that there's room for abuse by those with access to the data. However, in some other locations, it's easier for governments to regulate and oversee how the data is used. For example, European ALPR data is protected by the region's General Data Protection Regulation, which is way more than we have here in the ALPR Wild West.

Recent findings suggest that in the U.S., Flock data from one municipality can be accessed by basically anyone in other areas with a Flock contract, and hackers who pulled a Flock camera apart revealed that it's pretty easy to get the stored data even without a contract. Some police officers have even been caught accessing Flock data after leaving the force, according to the Washington Post. When this happens, finding accountability can be hard. ALPRs owned and run by the state directly at least have clear channels for voicing dissent, though it may also be true that they're more entrenched and harder to remove.

It spent surprisingly little time plugged in.

According to recent reports, BMW used an i3 50 xDrive to cover the 3,658 miles (5,886.7 kilometers) from Norway’s North Cape to Tarifa, Spain, charging for precisely 2 hours, 45 minutes and 54 seconds. BMW says that beats the previous Paneuropeana record, set in 2017, by over seven hours.

According to recent reports, the challenge is to cross Europe north to south spending as little time charging as possible. Drivers must pass through set checkpoints, but they can choose their route and where to charge. BMW used public chargers, averaging 275 kW during charging stops.

So, how'd BMW pull it off? Chalk it up to a combination of high-powered charging, long range, and strong efficiency, all enabled by the automaker's new 800-volt Neue Klasse EV tech.

On the road, the i3 used just 12.5 kWh/100 km (around 5 miles per kWh), meaning each charging stop provided a lot of mileage. With that consumption, the i3’s 108.7 kilowatt-hour battery would deliver 540 miles (869 km) of real-world driving range before hitting 0%. That's quite a bit more than the i3 50 xDrive's 468-mile EPA rating with 20-inch summer tires. The record-breaking i3 had 19-inch aero wheels and low-rolling-resistance tires, which certainly helped.

Remarkably, the 75-hour trip wasn't some slog at low speeds either. BMW reports an average speed of 79.7 km/h, or 49.5 mph.

Recent findings suggest that the i3 sedan features BMW’s sixth-generation electric drive technology, including an 800-volt architecture and cylindrical battery cells arranged in a cell-to-pack design. It also supports bidirectional charging, with a peak DC charging rate of 400 kW. BMW quotes a 10–80% time of 21 minutes and claims it can add up to 263 miles (423 km) of WLTP range in 10 minutes.

Industry observers note that BMW has already demonstrated the Neue Klasse platform’s long-range ability by driving an iX3 from Hungary to Germany. The 626-mile (1,007 km) journey took a production iX3 from Debrecen to Munich without recharging, arriving with 2% battery remaining. That required preparation, mostly country-road driving and switching off systems, including air conditioning. Impressive, certainly, but not how I’d choose to spend every road trip.

Sources indicate that my iX3 drive across Romania and over the Transfăgărășan involved considerably less restraint. I wanted to enjoy the car on a great road, which meant Sport mode and enthusiastic mountain driving. I liked the climb enough to do it twice, and its significant battery and impressive efficiency helped stave off range anxiety.

After roughly 250 miles (400 km) on the second day, including the mountain driving and the return to Bucharest, I got home with 16% remaining without charging that day. I proved that with one of the latest long-range EVs, you can skip an inconvenient charger, take a detour, or enjoy a mountain road without making the battery the main character of your holiday.

Recent findings suggest that long-distance EV road trips across Europe are already much easier than many people realize. Taking part in Eurocharge 2025, I drove more than 3,000 miles across the continent in several different EVs, and finding a working fast charger was rarely a concern. We even covered 700 miles in a single day, with charging fitting around shopping and food stops.

Recent findings suggest that you don’t need record-breaking range or a team of BMW engineers to make these journeys straightforward. The infrastructure already makes them pretty easy, and high-tech cars like the fresh i3 mean you can spend even less of your trip plugged in.

#81. This Honda Civic Is The Direct Ancestor Of The OG Tesla Roadster

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1607 w)
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik

This Honda Civic Is The Direct Ancestor Of The OG Tesla Roadster

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1607 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tom Gage is the one-time CEO of a firm you probably don't remember, called AC Propulsion.
  • See, underneath its aged sheet metal, it wasn't a Civic at all, but more of a science experiment.
  • It has been revealed that we interviewed Gage, who explained that it wasn't electric propulsion (at first) that attracted Tesla co-founder Martin Eberhard to EVs — and, eventually, Elon Musk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tom Gage is the one-time CEO of a firm you probably don't remember, called AC Propulsion. However, that firm was one of the progenitors of EVs and, by extension, Tesla. Gage is also the one-time owner of this 1994 Honda Civic. This past weekend he sold it, and we should explain why that's important.

See, underneath its aged sheet metal, it wasn't a Civic at all, but more of a science experiment. It has no tailpipe because Gage's partner, AC Propulsion co-founder Alan Cocconi, gutted the little hatchback in 1994 to fill with lead-acid bricks and convert the Civic into a proof-of-concept electric car that led to the rise of Tesla. The Tesla link is that AC Propulsion used the Civic to try out systems that would later debut on the manufacturer's 1998 tzero electric Roadster. That car looked cooler, but had the same tech that powered the electric Honda. And it's that technology that Tesla eventually licensed in 2004 and that ended up featuring in the original Tesla Roadster in 2008.

It has been revealed that we interviewed Gage, who explained that it wasn't electric propulsion (at first) that attracted Tesla co-founder Martin Eberhard to EVs — and, eventually, Elon Musk. It was actually its sexy shape, which was just a kit car called the Piontek Sportech. "I mean, that was exactly the reason we built the tzero in the first place," Gage explains. "EVs still had this golf cart image, and so even with lead-acid batteries, the tzero would be zero to 60 in the four-second range." This is funny because, actually, the Honda was just as fast. The tale of how AC Propulsion went from gutting Civics to making electric Scions and, eventually, helping spawn the iconic Tesla Roadster, is fascinating. It even includes a bit of spying, too.

Some of Cocconi's engineering that made it into this 1994 Honda Civic was way ahead of its time. For instance, Gage claims Cocconi devised a module that could produce AC-to-DC (and vice-versa) power flow. "When you were driving, [it] could take the DC current from the battery and convert it to high-frequency AC to run the motor. And when you weren't driving, and you plugged it in, the same inverter components would convert the AC from the grid into DC to charge the battery.".

Modern EVs have this capability, but even today, something Cocconi worked on isn't ubiquitous — feeding power from the EV back to your home or to the grid. AC Propulsion cars were eventually capable of that at up to 20 kilowatts, while the 2027 Ford Fathom will be able to do this without a wall inverter at 10 kW.

Industry observers note that according to Gage, the Civic had the first iteration of the 200-horsepower system, which the firm called a power electronics unit because it was more than just the motor and inverter. It contained that, as well as the charger, and the ability to push out a 12-volt DC power supply, which the Civic (or any car) needs since all of its components run on 12 volts.

It has been revealed that even back in the 1990s, AC Propulsion was looking for solutions that still bedevil carmakers today. For instance, how do you get reasonable all-electric range and fight battery weight simultaneously? At first, because the manufacturer was working with lead-acid batteries, they were stuck with limited range, and those batteries were far heavier than later lithium cells. Gage indicates that with batteries aboard, the Civic exceeded the gross vehicle limit of what the chassis was designed for, with the batteries alone weighing 1,200 pounds.

Fixing this required fitting a trailer with a gas engine aboard to operate as a range-extending generator, which topped up the batteries while driving. This created a series hybrid rather than a parallel hybrid, and the difference is that series hybrids only run their gas motors as generators — the engines don't power the wheels. Hence, putting the motor on a trailer works just fine. "We had several generations," Gage laughed. "We had some kind of a Generac standard generator, which we modified in various ways, but the exhaust was really stinky and [it] didn't have that much power.".

They eventually turned to Kawasaki, using the engine from the Ninja 250, which cranked at 11,000 rpm. "It was a little noisy," Gage quips. But it enabled the little Honda to get a remarkable 81 mpg. Later, AC Propulsion would adopt lithium-ion laptop batteries, and finally they could ditch needing to tow a gasoline engine to power an electric motor.

Recent findings suggest that AC Propulsion went from their lead-acid-battery Civic in 1994 to the tzero in 1998. It initially also ran on lead-acid batteries. That problem was eventually solved in 2003, when AC Propulsion adopted lithium-ion batteries for the tzero. And this was huge for performance and range. "That was what drew the attention of the founders of Tesla," Gage says, referring to Tesla co-founder Martin Eberhard. "Just getting the lithium-ion batteries, the tzero went from 80 to a 100-mile range to a 300-mile range with a 600-pound weight reduction.".

In a recent development, eberhard became an early investor in AC Propulsion and wanted to purchase one of the tzeros. But mass production, according to Gage, was out of the question, since the cars would have to sell for $220,000, and AC Propulsion told Eberhard they were losing $100,000 on every tzero they made. But Eberhard still had sports car dreams, which turned out to be fortunate for him. Around this time, Gage and Cocconi were trying to attract another investor, a man named Elon Musk. They didn't want Musk's money to make more tzeros, but to transform the future of transportation.

"What the world really needs is a low-cost, high-utility vehicle," Gage says. But Musk, like Eberhard, didn't care about cars for the masses. "It was too mundane for him," Gage recalls. "He wanted to do something like the tzero. So I introduced him to Martin [Eberhard]." That's how Tesla got started. From 2004, rather than outright build Teslas, AC Propulsion would license its tzero technology to the startup. This would later help spawn the 2008 Tesla Roadster — the predecessor to the new Roadster that's boring and doesn't really fly, according to your takes.

Sources indicate that gage and Cocconi's next significant idea wouldn't turn out to be anything as consequential as they'd hoped. They were converting Scion xBs into EVs, and AC Propulsion called that car the eBox. Gage explains they chose the Scion because it was practical and cheap. "It's got some of the best rear seat ingress and egress of any car ever built, in my opinion. Maybe that's a small thing, but you know, it was just a super utilitarian design." As Gage also explains, that Scion seemed "iconoclastic." And there was the matter of a tall-riding box, the better for stuffing batteries aboard. Unfortunately, the second-generation xB was a lot heavier than the first. "We realized the importance of lightweight to make the end product as good as it could be," he claims, so they explored working with Nissan instead.

It has been revealed that nissan did oblige — but with an ulterior motive, according to Gage. "They ended up sending a bunch of engineers over several times to drive the eBox and look at it. We thought we were trying to work a deal with them where they would provide us with rolling chassis or some kind of supply arrangement." But that's not what Gage suspects was actually happening. "Turns out, what they were really doing was scoping out what we were doing," because Nissan was researching its own EV. "Then a year or two later, they came out with the Leaf." The Leaf is still on the market, and Nissan recently came out with a Leaf Nismo.

There's a kicker to this story. Gage worked in the battery division of AC Propulsion until 2011, and he noticed that the Civic was just gathering dust. So he bought it for $100. "I forget when they stopped driving it, but it was just parked in the back lot. I offered them 100 bucks for it, and they sold it." Not that it was a gem, or even running, Gage explains. "One of the employees at one point asked if he could turn it into a race car, and he started to tear it apart, but that's about as far as he got.".

According to recent reports, gage says that this employee's ambitious plan included rewiring it and making a different adapter for the battery pack to switch from lead-acid to lithium-ion batteries. "I just know they wanted to get rid of it, and so I took it on, and I've been storing it ever since here," meaning at his house in Southern California. He thought about switching over from lead-acid to lithium-ion, which he figured would yield a car with up to 600 miles of range. He also thought of just going for broke with, "Super high-power lithium batteries, and then have a bit of a rocket ship, you know, because it would be much lighter than the average EV would and still have 200 horsepower.".

Recent findings suggest that whether that's the Civic's destiny is unclear. But the good news is that the buyer already owns an AC Propulsion car, a Honda CRX the company converted in the early '90s. Gage called him a "worthy buyer." To this, we can only add that we hope there's another chapter to this story when the Civic is once again burning rubber under electric power.

  • Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe and hardware chief Vidya Rajagopalan explained the situation during an interview with the venture capital firm Kleiner Perkins.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rivian is hoping to cash in on the AI boom through its work on a new in-car assistant, highly automated driving features, and a new robotics project. The data center frenzy is also complicating things for the EV startup by making previously commonplace components pricier and harder to source.

Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe and hardware chief Vidya Rajagopalan explained the situation during an interview with the venture capital firm Kleiner Perkins.

"Hardware is hard in ways that I think people don’t fully always appreciate until you’re in it," Scaringe mentioned, adding that it takes thousands of suppliers—and suppliers to suppliers—to build a car.

Today, Rivian is having a more challenging time sourcing commodity components like memory chips, Scaringe mentioned, as insatiable demand from AI players sends prices skyrocketing.

Recent findings suggest that "Three years ago, we were not spending a lot of time thinking about memory. It was a commodity," he said. "And now an enormous amount of time goes into planning for memory, optimizing it at the board level, how we’re using it, and then really thinking strategically about how we source it.".

It has been revealed that A shortage of memory chips, particularly DRAM, or dynamic random access memory, is rippling throughout the tech world. DRAM manufacturers are directing capacity toward higher-margin sales to AI firms, creating bottlenecks for other industries like automotive. Apple blamed the data center-driven run up in memory costs when it hiked prices for its laptops and other devices earlier this year.

In a recent development, and auto players have been sounding the alarm too. In a filing earlier this year, China's Li Auto called out "significant supply tightness and price volatility in memory components, such as DRAM and NAND flash, which are essential for our smart cockpit and autonomous driving systems." Both GM and Ford noted higher memory costs on recent earnings calls, and both announced long-term supply deals with Micron this summer.

On Rivian's latest earnings call, Scaringe said Rivian is looking for ways to offset the rising costs of memory chips and other commodity components so it can hit the R2's advertised base price of $45,000.

Recent findings suggest that it isn't just memory that's causing headaches for Rivian. "We deal with this all the time, supply chain shortages, it's a bane of our existence," Rajagopalan stated. "With the data center boom, a lot of the e-glass for [printed circuit boards] is really hard to find. And so you could have a component shortage in one space that totally throws you off." Multilayer ceramic capacitors (MLCCs), a basic circuit-board component, are another thing Rivian didn't pay much mind to before.

Sources indicate that "MLCC capacitors, you never thought about them. You’re thinking about them now, right?" she said.

The tough environment comes as Rivian is ramping up its own AI and tech efforts with an in-house processor that's set to hit consumer R2s next year. Rivian says the RAP1 chip, along with a upcoming lidar sensor, will help R2s achieve higher and higher levels of automated driving in the coming years.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, volkswagen is getting ready to launch a latest electric car starting at about €20,000 ($22,000) in 2027, and it looks like the entry-level EV may no longer be nameless. A newly filed trademark could have just given away what VW aims to call it.

The newly introduced entry-level EV is “the last piece of the puzzle,” Volkswagen brand CEO Thomas Schäfer stated last March after unveiling the ID. EVERY1 concept car.

Volkswagen stated the production version will launch in 2027 with a starting price of around €20,000 ($22,000).

According to recent reports, the new model will sit below the ID. Polo in Volkswagen’s Electric Urban Car Family, a lineup of compact, affordable electric cars.

In a recent development, volkswagen’s current entry-level EV lineup includes the ID. Polo, ID. Cross, the Cupra Raval, and Skoda Epiq, all based on its upcoming MEB+ platform.

After launching the lower-priced standard versions of the ID. Polo and ID. Cross recently, starting at €24,995 and €27,995, respectively, Volkswagen is preparing to launch an even smaller, more affordable EV next year.

A recent trademark filing with the European Union Intellectual Property Office (EUIPO) and the German DPMA may have just revealed the name of VW’s upcoming €20,000 EV.

It has been revealed that volkswagen filed a trademark application for the name ID. UP on October 22, 2026, with the EUIPO and DPMA, suggesting this will be the name of the upcoming electric car in 2027.

The trademark follows previous reports that VW planned to revive the former Up! name as part of its shift away from its previous numerical naming scheme (ID.3, ID.4, ID.5, etc.).

According to recent reports, volkswagen has kept most details a secret thus far. Like the ID. Polo, the first to go on sale with an established VW nameplate, the ID. UP is expected to use the same 37 kWh LFP battery to reduce costs.

It has been revealed that the VW ID. Polo with the 37 kWh battery offers a WLTP range of up to 334 km (207 miles), so the smaller ID. UP will likely provide around the same, if not slightly more.

Volkswagen noted it will offer at least 250 km (155 miles) of range. It will also use a latest 70 kW (94 hp) electric motor, enabling a top speed of 130 km/h (80 mph).

The production version of the ID. EVERY1, expected to arrive as the ID. UP, will be one of nine new models VW plans to launch by 2027.

According to recent reports, volkswagen previously mentioned the entry-level EV will be 3,880 mm long, which would position it between the former Up! (3,600 mm) and the ID. Polo (4,053 mm). Despite its compact size, VW said the electric city car will seat four passengers and offer a luggage compartment volume of 305 liters.

The VW Group’s new Electric Urban Car Family is off to a strong start, securing nearly 150,000 orders after series production began in June.

All models within the family are built on the MEB+ platform with a FWD powertrain, and share more than 80% of the components and tech.

Volkswagen said the production version of the ID. EVERY1 will be among the first vehicles based on its zonal, software-defined vehicle (SDV) architecture, which it is developing through its joint venture with Rivian.

Ah, finally a car in the upper range of being meaningful and sensible.

If someone needs more, then those are obviously special needs people. Being like can't enter and exit such a sensible car. Or like having to move the 15 horses of their 5 daughters. Or being a fieldworker driving a gazillion miles every day. Or requiring a lot of attention from lesser beings.

Industry observers note that in March, the Rivian and Volkswagen Group Technologies (RV Tech) joint venture tested the new SDV architecture on the ID. EVERY1, alongside Audi and Scout reference vehicles, validating over-the-air (OTA) capabilities.

The fresh architecture will enable “highly automated driving features” and “advanced infotainment solutions,” with continuous OTA updates.

While VW said it will deploy the SDV architecture in “electric vehicles across markets in the Western Hemisphere,” the entry-level EV is not expected to reach the States.

Hummer H1s May Be Nearly Indestructible, But Some Serious Flaws Live In That 'Nearly' Part

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the Hummer brand officially rolled out in 1992 with the debut of its AM General High Mobility Multipurpose Wheeled Vehicle military-based civilian model.
  • Sources indicate that when it comes to imposing four-wheeled machines, there's nothing quite as eye-catching and road-commanding as the original Hummer.
  • It has been revealed that because of its high profile and rarity, every variant of the H1 generally still commands a pretty penny, even two decades after production ended.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the Hummer brand officially rolled out in 1992 with the debut of its AM General High Mobility Multipurpose Wheeled Vehicle military-based civilian model. Much like the popularity of the Willys Jeep in post-WWII America, the H1 capitalized on rah-rah post-Gulf War nationalism and a personal endorsement from Arnold Schwarzenegger to find its place in the automotive zeitgeist. After being awarded its first military production contract in 1983, the substantial diesel-powered machine was well-proven by the time John Q. Public could place an order a decade later. If the HMMWV can be relied on by our fighting finest in the Muthanna Province, then surely it'll withstand the rigors of your suburban commute, right? Well, as it turns out, the answer is a cryptically Schrödinger-esque yes and no.

Sources indicate that when it comes to imposing four-wheeled machines, there's nothing quite as eye-catching and road-commanding as the original Hummer. Between 1992 and 1999, the vehicle was sold in small quantities by AM General's civilian division, but General Motors purchased the rights to market and distribute the Hummer brand for the latest millennium. With just shy of 12,000 units sold across the truck's entire production run, these things are a bit thin on the ground, but they maintain a strong cultural significance today, and the appeal of a genuine mil-spec vehicle is hard to deny.

It has been revealed that because of its high profile and rarity, every variant of the H1 generally still commands a pretty penny, even two decades after production ended. A high-mileage early non-turbo diesel model might bring as low as $35,000, while a low-mileage 2006-only H1 Alpha runs into the low six-figure range. If you're going to be spending that much money to get yourself one of these rolling monuments of gender-affirming care, what trouble should you expect and look out for? Let's dig into it.

The first issue is that, simply due to their size and material density, they're really heavy. At around 7,500 pounds, you're moving a lot of metal around. Weight translates to atrocious fuel economy, like about 10 miles per gallon bad. Another downside: due to the military-based nature of these trucks, driver comfort is hardly a concern, and the noise, vibration, and harshness engineers were not really consulted in the design phase. According to a Hagerty review, the "engine sounds like a jackhammer inside the cockpit." Oh, and it doesn't have airbags.

Recent findings suggest that on the plus side, a Hummer H1 is mostly indestructible, except for one major flaw. If you're a long-time reader of Jalopnik, you'll probably know where this is going, because over a decade ago our own Doug Demuro found out firsthand what breaks on the Hummer H1. I'll let him explain it.

"Beginning in about 1996, every single Hummer was fitted with a 6.5-liter Detroit Diesel turbodiesel V8, which combined the 194 horsepower of a Toyota Camry with the 438 lb-ft of torque from an angry farm tractor.

Well, there was one little issue: every single one of these engines was manufactured with a casting flaw that resulted in a crack on the number eight cylinder. Fortunately, the fix was easy: you just replaced the engine.

But check this out: it affected every single Hummer manufactured from 1996 to 2000... Every single Hummer built from 1996 to 2000 has either had its engine fail due to the number eight cylinder concern, or will have its engine fail.".

It has been revealed that the pre-1996 non-turbo Detroit Diesel-powered models, the rare gasoline-powered model, and the 2001-2006 models are unaffected. Check the engine casting number and make sure it was made after March 15, 1999.

Industry observers note that there is another major issue with Hummer H1 trucks, but it's significantly less catastrophic than a failed engine. The onboard tire inflation-deflation system leaks because, of course, it does. Especially after a couple of decades of sitting on display with low-mileage odometers, the rubber lines of the system tend to crack and drop pressure. It's possible to replace all of the lines and make it function again, and there are ways to bypass the system altogether and inflate your tires the old-fashioned way.

Sources indicate that there are plenty of other issues that come with buying a twenty-year-old truck. Just like anything with decades of wear, keep an eye on worn suspension components, leaks, rust, ill-maintained brakes, and maintenance records. According to TireRack.com, a set of H1 tires will cost up to $2,240, so that information might help you negotiate. Also, because this is a rare machine, you probably won't find any of the parts you need for things like the tire inflation system at your local corner parts store. The parts exist, but you might want to keep the Hummer Parts Guy on speed dial.

Recent findings suggest that there are plenty of options for '96 to 2000 trucks that haven't had their engines replaced yet. If you can get one for cheap, it might make the basis of an interesting project truck. I'm imagining a rare two-door pickup H1s with a Duramax "Mongoose" 8.3-liter turbo diesel V8, the one found in the current Chevrolet and GMC HD trucks making 555 horsepower and 1,230 lb-ft of torque. That might be the only way to make an actually fast Hummer.

The Test Bed For Jaguar's XJ220 Twin-Turbo V6 Was A Ford Transit Van

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, jaguar is in a strange place right now because it's wedged between two very different versions of itself.
  • Recent findings suggest that then there's the XJ220 — arguably the most curious chapter of them all.
  • In a recent development, what's interesting about its twin-turbo V6 is how it was tested.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, jaguar is in a strange place right now because it's wedged between two very different versions of itself. In front lies a future defined by a bold design language and electric powertrains, ushered in by perhaps the most divisive car in a generation: the 1,015-hp, 400-mile 2028 Type 01 sedan. Behind it is a century-old story about craftsmanship, passion, and a great big dollop of supercharger whine. There was the absolutely stunning E-Type, which Enzo Ferrari famously christened as the most beautiful car in the world, and let's not forget the bonkers V12-powered XJR-9 that not only won Le Mans, but was voted as one of your favorite sports prototype race cars of all time.

Recent findings suggest that then there's the XJ220 — arguably the most curious chapter of them all. It had a difficult start to life because Jaguar opted for a last-minute switch from a V12 to a twin-turbo V6 and from all-wheel drive to rear-wheel drive, instantly making it less sexy and appealing to customers than rivals like the Bugatti EB110 and Ferrari F40. Instead, the XJ220 did its talking with sheer force, clocking a 217-mph top speed to become the world's fastest production car in 1992. Imagine how smug its engineers felt.

In a recent development, what's interesting about its twin-turbo V6 is how it was tested. We all know manufacturers use test mule cars to iron out any pre-production complications, but these normally have some sort of resemblance to the final car. For the XJ220, Jaguar and its development partner Tom Walkinshaw Racing (TWR) decided to use a humble Ford Transit. Yes, a Ford Transit. If you're thinking this sounds familiar, it's because it was the same vehicle Richard Hammond used in a drag race against a Holden Maloo truck, when the original "Top Gear" trio competed against their Aussie counterparts.

Most likely, discretion. The XJ220 was a tight-lipped secret around the Jaguar offices, and when TWR had finalized the engine setup and wanted to run its various litmus tests, it had to do so very carefully. So, what better to use to disguise your shiny new, world-record-chasing motor than something absolutely nobody would suspect?

Based on a 1989 long-wheelbase Ford Transit, the exterior looked almost identical to a slightly worn example, with the only potential giveaway being the ZR performance tires and identical alloy wheels to those that would eventually end up on the XJ220. But if you were to open up the cargo bed, you'd spot the 3.5-liter twin-turbo V6 — originally rated at 540 horsepower — and suspiciously racy running gear lurking low down.

It has been revealed that an interesting fact is that this engine is actually closely related to the engine in the MG 6R4 — a monstrous rally car, and arguably the only cool car MG has ever built. You see, the 6R4 was built for Group B, which ended in 1986, and thus meant MG had no use for a properly decked-out six-cylinder engine anymore. It then reportedly sold the rights and design infrastructure to TWR, and that's how it eventually wound up in the XJ220.

If you thought it was heading for a peaceful retirement in the Scottish Highlands, you'd be dead wrong. Once TWR had finished work with it, the Transit was acquired by the Benetton Formula 1 team, which used it as a parts delivery vehicle. It might have been on the verge of being scrapped after Benetton was done with it, but then, in stepped a savior: Don Law Racing.

Don Law Racing is widely considered to be the world's leading XJ220 specialist. The rightful heir to the Frankenstein Transit project, then. The tech giant worked on the vehicle and got it back up to condition, and once it eventually did, it appeared in places like the Goodwood Festival of Speed, where it has indeed been up the hill on multiple occasions and left unsuspecting spectators in awe. Quite the fairy-tale ending, wouldn't you say?

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla will now make the Cybertruck for a little while longer to fulfill more orders, Elon Musk said on Wednesday.

"In order to work through more of the Cybertruck order backlog, production will be extended through the end of summer 2027," he remarked in an X post, adding in a reply, "This is not the smartest move from a profit-maximizing standpoint btw, but there must be some room in this world for sentimentality or what’s the point?".

Industry observers note that in a late-night tweet last week, Musk declared the forthcoming demise of the stainless-steel pickup in the middle of next year to make more room for production of steering wheel-free Cybercabs at Tesla's Texas factory. He later clarified that the truck would be made for eight more months, pointing to an expiration date of July 2027 for what is surely the strangest and most polarizing pickup ever made.

Recent findings suggest that now production is poised to last through most of September, giving the Cybertruck a roughly 10-month runway. Musk had previously said Tesla would have to return some deposits as it wouldn't be able to deliver all the trucks customers had ordered before production came to a close.

Elon Musk stated Tesla is extending Cybertruck production so it can fulfill more orders.

It's still an untimely end for a model that attracted more controversy than cold, hard sales. Musk once targeted an annual output of 250,000 trucks, which would make it a top seller in the pickup market. Tesla ended up selling some 70,000 of them, per industry estimates, since sales kicked off at the end of 2023.

In part, extending the truck's production run may be a way to placate Tesla's die-hard fans, some of whom expressed outrage at the decision to cancel it so suddenly and unceremoniously. Say what you will about the truck itself, but it has amassed a loyal following like few other vehicles have. Over 5,000 people have signed a petition to keep the Cybertruck in production. Unplugged Performance, which makes Tesla accessories, stated it's trying to get investors on board to take over Cybertruck production from Tesla.

Now those Tesla devotees have a little more time to buy a Cybertruck. It'll cost them dearly, though. Since announcing the truck's cancelation, Tesla made the top-trim, tri-motor Cyberbeast the only one available—and hiked its price to $110,000.

#74. Mini Truck Vs. Side-By-Side: What Are The Practical Differences?

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1934 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik

Mini Truck Vs. Side-By-Side: What Are The Practical Differences?

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1934 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You've likely seen those neat little mini trucks from Japan.
  • President Trump was quite smitten with Kei trucks when he saw them in Japan, apparently for the first time, later calling them "really cute." And in a December 2025 Truth Social post, he mentioned that he had "approved" the manufacture of these "tiny" vehicles here.
  • Sources indicate that maybe you're thinking about snagging one of these trucks for your farm, ranch, or construction site and wondering how they compare to those side-by-sides that are made for work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You've likely seen those neat little mini trucks from Japan. They're the size of a compact vehicle, but have a bed as long as some full-size pickups. These Kei trucks, as they are called, look like they would be pretty practical for a number of uses.

President Trump was quite smitten with Kei trucks when he saw them in Japan, apparently for the first time, later calling them "really cute." And in a December 2025 Truth Social post, he mentioned that he had "approved" the manufacture of these "tiny" vehicles here. But, as is the case with many of the president's statements, no one is quite sure what that means. Unfortunately, you can't buy a fresh one for road use in the U.S., but older ones are available thanks to an exception in import laws.

Sources indicate that maybe you're thinking about snagging one of these trucks for your farm, ranch, or construction site and wondering how they compare to those side-by-sides that are made for work. These utility task vehicles (UTVs) also have a bed on the back and are often used to haul small loads around on a worksite. There are several differences. For one thing, you can easily find newly introduced UTVs for sale. Their payload and towing capacities are often higher than those of most Kei trucks. They are built more for off-roading, while Kei trucks are built for the street. It really comes down to what your needs are, though.

In a recent development, kei trucks were not made to meet U.S. safety and environmental standards. The Clean Air Act prohibits importing a vehicle that doesn't meet federal emissions standards unless it's at least 21 years old. Federal law also bans foreign vehicles less than 25 years old that don't meet safety standards.

It has been revealed that newer Kei trucks can be imported only as off-road vehicles, permanently limited to 25 mph. That means if you want one for the road, you're stuck shopping for used Kei trucks that are at least 25 years old. That's not to say they're hard to find. Type "used Kei truck for sale" into Google and you'll see several listings for Kei trucks, as well as businesses that sell them. And the ones we've seen look to be in better shape than the typical 25- or 30-year-old vehicle, on the outside at least.

According to recent reports, it's a bit more straightforward with UTVs, or side-by-sides. They are off-road vehicles, so they are perfectly legal to sell brand-newly introduced in the U.S. We found 25 Polaris dealerships and at least 30 Honda Powersports dealerships in the state of Florida alone. Of course, there are plenty of used side-by-sides all over the place, as well. Sites like ATV Trader, ATVHunt, and Autotrader all contain several listings.

Industry observers note that you're going to get a longer, more versatile bed with a mini truck than you will with a UTV. Anyone can see that just by looking at the two vehicles. Kei truck beds are often over 6 feet long and over 4 feet wide. With the tailgate down, that's big enough to haul a piece of plywood or drywall, with just a little bit hanging over the edge.

The sides of a Kei truck's bed often fold down, allowing for easy loading of a packed pallet by a forklift. The walls are not very high, which makes it easier to load and offload the bed, as well. Beds on UTVs are often much smaller, with the boxes on some models being around 3.5 feet in length and a little over 4 feet in width.

Don't confuse bed size with payload capacity, however. Kei trucks, as regulated by the Japanese government, can carry no more than 771 pounds of cargo. On the other hand, the Polaris Ranger XD 1500 has a box capacity of 1,500 pounds, which is on the high end for UTVs. We should point out, though, that payload capacity is the final word on how much you can load into your vehicle. The total weight of passengers in the cab and cargo in the box should not exceed payload capacity, regardless of box capacity.

It has been revealed that comparing the towing capacities of mini trucks and side-by-sides is tricky because there aren't any official towing capacities published for Kei trucks. Japan's registration calculation caps the total weight of a brakeless trailer at half of the truck's curb weight. That puts the limit for an unbraked trailer at around 700 to 800 pounds for an older Kei truck, including the trailer.

According to recent reports, that's as close as you can get without a written capacity from the manufacturer. You will find people online who insist they can tow more with their Kei truck, but just because some random person claims to have regularly towed over 1,000 pounds without wrecking their Kei truck doesn't mean that you should try it with yours. Nor should you go by the rated capacity of an aftermarket tow hitch. That is the rating of the tow hitch, not of your vehicle. Overall, it's best to stick to light towing when it comes to Kei trucks.

In a recent development, on the other hand, the towing capacities of UTVs are typically straightforward. You'll find the capacities listed in their specs, and those specs vary from model to model. For example, the Polaris Ranger XD 1500 NorthStar is rated to tow 3,500 pounds, while the Honda Pioneer 520 is rated to tow 1,000 pounds. If your towing needs involve heavy loads, UTVs are probably the way to go.

Recent findings suggest that you can use either type of vehicle off-road. This is where side-by-sides shine, though, as they were designed specifically for handling rough terrain. Let's start with the tires. You can see from pictures of Kei trucks that they usually come fitted with small street tires that look like they belong on a compact car. UTV tires, on the other hand, often look like tractor tires or tires that go on an ATV. They are made to kick up mud and to laugh at messy terrain.

Clearance is another difference between mini trucks and side-by-sides. The Suzuki Carry mini truck has a ground clearance of around 6 inches. However, the ground clearance for the Honda Pioneer 520 side-by-side is 8.7 inches. The ground clearance for the Polaris Ranger XP 1000 is 14 inches. Of course, the drivetrain is also important when it comes to handling off-road terrain. It's not hard to find a used Kei truck with 4WD. UTVs are typically equipped with AWD, and some can switch between multiple drive modes.

While UTVs excel at off-road performance, we can't say that Kei trucks have to stick to the street. The inclusion of 4WD allows them to hold their own. They are well suited for hard-packed soil, gravel roads, some construction sites, and level ground. But if you have really rough, uneven ground, deep muddy ruts, large rocks, and other obstacles to deal with, our money is on the UTVs.

It probably seems obvious that mini trucks would hold the advantage when it comes to street legality. After all, Kei trucks were made for streets, while side-by-sides were made for off-roading. It's not that simple, though. Sure, the federal government allows Kei trucks that are at least 25 years old to be imported, but that doesn't mean they are road-legal in your state.

Colorado, for example, does not at the moment allow Kei vehicles to be registered or titled, but that changes on January 1, 2028. After that, Kei vehicles will be allowed on Colorado roads that have a speed limit of 55 miles per hour or less. Pennsylvania allows mini trucks to be registered only with an off-road title, with a farm exemption, or with an antique registration, unless the owner holds a grandfathered registration from 2021. Imported Kei vehicles at least 25 years old are now fully road-legal in Alaska.

Side-by-sides are actually street-legal in certain states. Arizona will issue a motorcycle-style plate to UTVs that have been specifically modified for street use. South Dakota has a similar law. In Colorado, counties and towns decide whether side-by-sides can use their roads, and some towns allow them only during certain hours. Trails are a different matter. The controlling authority for each patch of land that has trails determines which kinds of vehicles are allowed on them. The bottom line is to check the laws of your locality before deciding which vehicle to purchase.

It has been revealed that in all of the excitement of finding a mini truck or buying a newly introduced side-by-side, it's easy to forget to think about the cost and time that need to go into maintaining these vehicles. Fortunately, maintenance isn't that hard for either type of vehicle. There are some things you want to consider, however.

In a recent development, the recommended frequency of maintenance for side-by-sides is similar to that of motorcycles. Polaris, for example, recommends that the first service for a new Ranger 1000 happen around the 25-hour or 500-mile mark and that the oil and filter then be changed every 200 hours, 2,000 miles, or year, whichever comes first. It's recommended to service the vehicle twice as frequently if it's been exposed to a lot of mud, water, or sand, which is kind of odd, considering that's exactly what side-by-sides are usually exposed to. One of the advantages of UTVs, though, is that you can buy one that is new enough to be under warranty.

Sources indicate that the service schedule for Kei trucks is generally not quite as frequent, and their simple engines are easy to work on. But we are talking about a 25-year-old vehicle here. Expect things to go wrong, like worn-out cooling systems, rusted parts of the frame, and vacuum lines that need replacing. Parts are surprisingly easy to find, though you may have to order some of them online. But most of us who work on our own cars have often done that, anyway.

It has been revealed that it's hard to compare apples to apples when we talk about the pricing for these vehicles. Any road-legal Kei truck you purchase in the U.S. will be at least 25 years old. It's not likely that you're going to look for a side-by-side that is that old. They are also built for different uses on different terrains.

You can find 25- to nearly 40-year-old Suzuki Carry trucks on Autotrader for anywhere from $7,000 to over $12,000. That's wild, considering you could get a brand-fresh Carry in Japan for around $7,500 to $10,000. On top of that, you're likely to have to make repairs right off the bat, since the truck is so old. A brand-new Polaris Ranger 1000 UTV costs more, starting around $15,000. But that comes with a 12-month warranty. We found late-model used UTVs on Autotrader and ATV Trader that were priced about the same as much older Kei trucks.

Recent findings suggest that so, which is the better deal? Who's to say? If you're just looking at age and wear and how it lines up with total cost, side-by-sides have a definite advantage. But that doesn't mean they represent the better deal for you personally. Paying a little more for a vehicle that is ideally suited for your uses is a better deal than paying less for a vehicle that doesn't quite fit your needs. Do your research, evaluate how and where you'll use the vehicle, and then make the purchase that's right for you.

The US Is Auctioning Seabed Near American Samoa. A $3 Million Bid Will Not Build a Mine.

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, on November 19, the US Marine Minerals Administration is scheduled to auction mineral rights covering about 31.5 million acres of seabed near American Samoa.
  • Recent findings suggest that the winning bidder will acquire a position from which to study mineral deposits and seek subsequent permissions.
  • The announcement is being treated as an American critical-minerals milestone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, on November 19, the US Marine Minerals Administration is scheduled to auction mineral rights covering about 31.5 million acres of seabed near American Samoa. The two areas have minimum bids of $3 million apiece, with 20-year lease terms. It is an impressive area and a modest opening price for a prospective fresh metals industry. The difference between the two numbers helps explain what the sale is actually offering.

Recent findings suggest that the winning bidder will acquire a position from which to study mineral deposits and seek subsequent permissions. The government has said explicitly that an issued lease does not authorize commercial harvesting. It allows preliminary work such as mapping, while physical exploration, testing and mining require additional plans and approvals. The lease does not establish reserves, a collector that can work for years, a processing plant or buyers willing to pay enough for the metals.

The announcement is being treated as an American critical-minerals milestone. Investors should pay close attention to the difference between a government auction and an operating mining project. A mineral lease can have speculative value long before a profitable business exists.

In my newly introduced TFIE Strategy Briefing on the American Samoa auction, I examine how federal leasing can advance while the integrated business case remains weak.

The acreage has no direct relationship to the amount of commercially recoverable metal. The final federal notice describes northern and southern areas of roughly 16.3 million and 15.2 million acres. They are regulatory boundaries. A mining organization needs deposit-grade and abundance data, continuity, recoverable tonnage, processing recoveries and a market price that leaves a margin after all the offshore and downstream costs.

The geology is becoming better understood. In April 2026, US Geological Survey scientists deployed 38 box cores in the Samoa Basin, of which 36 yielded enough material for nodule-density measurements. The expedition report is useful upcoming evidence about the region. It is an expedition summary rather than a reserve statement for either lease area. Mineral distributions vary within the sampled region, and the better-studied Clarion-Clipperton Zone is not an adequate substitute for American Samoa’s own geological evidence.

Collection creates another set of costs. Impossible Metals proposes autonomous vehicles that select nodules and return to a support vessel. The Metals Organization uses a more mature crawler-and-riser approach that has demonstrated recovery at pilot scale. Both must turn offshore demonstrations into dependable annual production, with maintenance, ship time, recovery systems and delays included. Their technologies should not be assigned the same engineering maturity, but neither has proved a profitable integrated mining-and-processing business.

In 2025, metallurgical engineer Lyle Trytten and I completed an independent techno-economic assessment commissioned by the National Ocean Protection Coalition. We examined both collection approaches, offshore operations, processing, metal markets and financial sensitivities. We judged commercial viability within the following 15 years highly unlikely. A new leasing process has not supplied the operating and financial evidence that was missing in that assessment.

In a recent development, the history of first-of-a-kind offshore production should influence the financing. Nautilus Minerals spent substantial capital on its Solwara-1 venture without reaching commercial production. Deep-sea mining depends on specialized machines, ships, handling systems, processing capacity and sales contracts working in sequence. The first production years of comparable projects are rarely smooth. The lease is one of the cheapest and earliest commitments in that chain.

American Samoa also has its own decision to make. Its government has supported scientific investigation while withholding support for commercial extraction at present. A lawsuit filed by Samoan chiefs and community groups contests the federal process. The resulting legal and territorial questions matter alongside engineering and economics. The environmental finding for preliminary leasing activities is not a finding about the effects of a future commercial mine.

Auction results will show what qualified bidders will pay for an opportunity. A winning bid can justify a company’s further studies and improve its fundraising story. An operating business will require years of capital investment, production evidence and profitable metal sales. Those are much harder milestones, and they remain ahead of the bidders.

Read A Seabed Lease Does Not Fix a Broken Business Case for the full assessment of the auction, and the Barnard–Trytten report for the underlying engineering and financial analysis.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rinnai has launched a new lineup of electric heat pump water heaters that adds wifi controls and more installation options to an appliance that can cut the energy needed for hot showers.

It has been revealed that the REHPW series comes in 50-, 65-, and 80-gallon sizes. It builds on Rinnai’s existing REHP lineup, with changes designed to make the units easier to install, monitor, and maintain.

Recent findings suggest that heat pump water heaters pull heat from the surrounding air and transfer it into the tank. Moving that heat requires less electricity than producing it with conventional electric resistance elements. There’s no fuel combustion at the appliance, although emissions from its electricity supply depend on the grid.

Industry observers note that rinnai lists a Uniform Energy Factor, or UEF, of 3.75 for the 50-gallon model and 4.0 for the two larger versions. Higher numbers mean greater efficiency under standardized testing; actual bills depend on electricity rates, hot water use, and installation conditions.

According to recent reports, the lineup delivers up to 91 gallons of hot water in the first hour, depending on tank size. That rating includes both stored hot water and what the unit can heat during that hour – useful context when several people take consecutive showers.

There are five operating modes, 4.5 kW backup heating elements, and a variable-speed fan designed to keep noise down. The heat pump can operate with ambient air as low as 37°F.

Installation is where some of the more practical upgrades show up.

Sources indicate that the newly introduced Rinnai heat pump water heater units have water connections on both the top and side, giving installers more options for connecting existing plumbing. Both the air intake and exhaust are on top, allowing zero side clearance where Rinnai’s installation requirements permit.

An optional ducting kit adds flexibility for tighter spaces. Carrying handles help with moving the tank into place, and the air filter slides out horizontally from the side for cleaning.

Rinnai has also added a third tank temperature sensor to the 50- and 80-gallon models to help manage hot water delivery.

In a recent development, wifi adds remote monitoring and control. Rinnai’s updated Central app supports the REHPW series, including scheduling and tools to use time-of-use electricity rates to manage energy use.

The units also carry CTA-2045 AC Level 2 certification for demand response. That gives compatible utility programs a way to communicate with the water heater and adjust its electricity use. Rinnai states the certification can help qualify homeowners for local and state utility demand-response rebates; availability depends on the program.

The series is Energy Star certified, meets NEEA Tier 4 requirements, and complies with California’s Title 24 requirements, including JA13, according to Rinnai. Warranty coverage includes 10 years for the tank and other parts, plus one year for labor.

It has been revealed that I’m very happy with my hybrid heat pump water heater. I run it in heat pump only mode in summer and it helps cool the house for free. For anyone on the fence, especially your utility offers a rebate, it’s definitely worth looking at.

Rinnai directs buyers to an installer for pricing, so the upfront cost – and how much a local rebate might offset it – will require a quote. However, the REHP series price on Amazon hovers around the $2,000 mark.

Sources indicate that something that would have been unimaginable five years ago is now reality. Google’s Gemini AI voice assistant can now be used on Apple CarPlay by iPhone customers, breaking some of the barriers that have traditionally been in place between the two tech giants.

In a recent development, starting today, Gemini users on iOS devices can open the app on CarPlay and pick up where they left off on their smartphone. The AI-powered chatbot can take multi-point questions and offer natural-sounding answers. That stated, after it’s front and center, Gemini can talk back and forth at the driver’s pace, even if it’s interrupted while it’s answering a question.

In a recent development, the American tech company said in an official blog post that Gemini on CarPlay can help the driver get ready for the day ahead. They can ask what’s on their calendar, when they need to leave for their next appointment, or talk through what they want to say before they arrive at a meeting.

It has been revealed that an inbox recap is also possible, as Gemini can connect to Google Workspace apps like Gmail and Google Calendar. Exploring local spots and landmarks while driving is also part of the chatbot’s feature list. All conversations on CarPlay are automatically synced to the Gemini app on the iPhone, so the driver can recap chats after they park.

Recent findings suggest that gemini on Apple CarPlay is rolling out globally to all Gemini users on iOS now. All supported Gemini Live languages are included. To get Gemini to pop up on CarPlay, the latest version of the app needs to be installed on the iPhone, microphone permissions need to be enabled, and Gemini Live needs to have been used at least once on the phone. If all of these prerequisites are met, the next time the iPhone is connected to CarPlay, the Gemini app will appear on the display, ready for a latest conversation or to pick up an old one.

The Gemini app’s CarPlay integration is just the latest move from Google to flood iPhones with its AI-enabled chatbot. Last month, the Alphabet-owned tech manufacturer embedded Gemini into the CarPlay mode of its Maps GPS navigation app.

Sources indicate that the year of the robotaxi rolls on. Just after writing about Zoox expanding its robotaxi service in Las Vegas, I see news that Zoox is entering Atlanta!

Industry observers note that “Our initial rollout will focus on the Northwest region of Atlanta, near Atlantic Station, Woodward, and Home Park. We will expand throughout the year as our testing progresses,” Zoox shares.

Recent findings suggest that to start with, in order to work out any bugs and avoid controversy, the service can only be used by Zoox employees, family members, and friends. But that should change fairly soon. “We look forward to opening our waitlist for Atlanta in the coming months, ahead of the launch of our Zoox Explorers early rider program.”.

I do find it interesting that Zoox, Waymo, and Tesla are all in a sort of fast (but sort of small) expansion phase at the same time. They each keep adding more cities, but with quite limited geographic ranges and vehicle fleets. Is it all the early budding of robotaxi services that will bloom into giant networks? Or is it companies rushing to try to prove their viability and build up economies of scale, but which might not actually be financially viable and profitable in the long run — or even next year? We’ll have to wait to see. In the meantime, it’s certainly exciting each time a new area is opened up and more electric robotaxis hit the road.

Recent findings suggest that in case you have forgotten where Zoox is in operation, the organization informs us: “Atlanta marks our newest testing market for the robotaxi. This is in addition to testing in Austin and Miami, our public service in Las Vegas, and our Zoox Explorers early rider program in San Francisco.”.

Also of note is the fact that Zoox didn’t just decide last month to go to Atlanta and rush into the market. It has been laying the groundwork for this launch for about a year and a half in the city. “We started operations in Atlanta in the Spring of 2025, using our testing fleet to map and learn about local driving behaviors, weather patterns, and the city infrastructure. Since then, we have been steadily expanding our driving capabilities, including beginning autonomous driving, and growing our geofence, fleet size, and team to prepare for this next stage of testing.” Zoox explains further how this is central to how Zoox operates:.

According to recent reports, “Zoox has always been thoughtful and measured in our approach to rolling out autonomous technology at every level. Before we even hit the road and begin driving with our testing fleet in any capacity, we first engage with local and state officials and regulators. Our philosophy is ‘no surprises’ as we lay the foundations for future service markets.

“Along with engaging with local and state officials and regulators, we also love partnering with the community. Workforce development starts long before a first job. That’s why we’re partnering with @Promise Center to help local youth learn, grow, and prepare for their futures in a safe, supportive environment. This partnership reflects our commitment to the Atlanta community. We’re excited to continue investing in the next generation and the future of this city.”.

According to recent reports, circling back to Atlanta and why the organization has made that one of the first cities for its robotaxi deployment, Zoox adds the following: “Atlanta is a dynamic, vibrant city. Known as the ‘Silicon Valley of the South,’ it boasts one of the largest ride-hailing markets in the United States. Atlanta’s dense, urban layout creates strong demand for efficient transportation solutions, which is where on-demand autonomous ride-hailing comes in. It also has a growing population, and demand like this is exactly why we’re excited to bring Zoox to Atlantans.”.

Lastly, as I also highlighted in my article last night about Zoox expanding in Las Vegas, one key thing Zoox is proud of and argues sets it apart from the competition is how vertically integrated its robotaxi business is and how useful the design of its vehicle is for its purpose. Here’s more: “While Atlanta has become a hub for autonomous testing, Zoox continues to stand apart from other companies. Unlike the retrofitted solutions currently on the road, our robotaxi was built from the ground up for fully autonomous ride-hailing. It has no steering wheel or driver’s seat, instead featuring spacious, carriage-style seating for up to four passengers. This design layout allows us to offer Zoox passengers more than just a ride; we are providing a private space where riders can socialize, relax, and reclaim their time. […].

“Zoox owns, operates, and assembles its vehicles, and is the only manufacturer currently deploying a fully driverless, purpose-built robotaxi on public roads in the U.S.

“We see promise in bringing our robotaxi service to Atlanta, and look forward to offering Atlantans this unique and private space to socialize, rock out, and create their own experience while being transported to their destination.”.

You can learn more on the Zoox website or the Zoox app.

#69. 5 Generations Of The Chevy Impala SS Ranked From Best To Worst Horsepower Ratings

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1248 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik

5 Generations Of The Chevy Impala SS Ranked From Best To Worst Horsepower Ratings

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1248 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mention a Chevy Impala, and thoughts of an unremarkable family sedan may come to mind, but add an SS next to the nameplate and things change.
  • It has been revealed that however, these horsepower numbers come with a catch.
  • Our ranking of every Impala SS generation by power takes into account the highest advertised horsepower ratings for regular-production SS models, regardless of whether it's gross or net.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mention a Chevy Impala, and thoughts of an unremarkable family sedan may come to mind, but add an SS next to the nameplate and things change. The Impala SS (Super Sport) is a pure horsepower play that dates back to 1961, two years after the Bowtie brand released the Impala as a standalone model. Its numbers are still impressive, even by 21st-century standards. The retail version of the Impala SS from the 1960s, which covered two generations, produced up to 425 horsepower. The later Impala SS generations from the 1990s and 2000s were less brutish, offering between 240 and 303 hp, but they were still a step up from their more mundane counterparts.

It has been revealed that however, these horsepower numbers come with a catch. The output figures for 1960s Impala SS models reflected gross horsepower ratings, which generally didn't account for intake, exhaust, and accessory loads. When the 1970s rolled around, the auto industry was dealing with tighter emissions regulations and insurance companies that took a dim view of high-powered cars. By the 1972 model year, Detroit switched to net horsepower calculations to better reflect real-world engine configurations. Because gross horsepower ratings often varied from manufacturer to manufacturer, there's no standard way to convert horsepower ratings between the methods, but both still measure horsepower at the crankshaft, not the wheels.

Our ranking of every Impala SS generation by power takes into account the highest advertised horsepower ratings for regular-production SS models, regardless of whether it's gross or net. Special race versions and modified cars are excluded. Here's how every Impala SS generation compares in maximum power output.

Recent findings suggest that the first Impala was a variant of the 1958 Bel Air, but the SS designation didn't arrive until the third-generation Impala in 1961. The second generation, without a Super Sport option, filled the two-year gap as the free-standing Impala model. The first Impala SS model's power output is a story of progression. The 1961 Impala SS arrived with a choice of V8 engines: 348-cubic-inch units rated at 305, 340, or 350 horsepower and a 409-cubic-inch V8 officially rated at 360 horsepower. In 1962, that king-of-the-hill powerplant could also be configured with dual four-barrel carburetors, increasing output to 409 horsepower.

Sources indicate that thanks to solid lifters, dual exhausts, and an 11:1 compression ratio, the 409's output rose to 425 gross horsepower for the 1963 model year. Chevy history buffs may also recall a 1963 Z11 lightweight drag-racing Impala with a 430-horsepower 427-cubic-inch V8. Keep in mind that this one wasn't a Super Sport model, nor was it a part of regular production, as only 57 were ever produced. The 1964 Impala SS continued with the same 409 from the previous year.

According to recent reports, horsepower for the second iteration of the Impala SS was in familiar territory, with peak outputs sitting at 425, but the Impala eventually took a different route to get there. To start, Chevy introduced an entirely new Impala with a sleeker exterior and a perimeter frame, ditching the X-type architecture of the outgoing model. The new looks helped the 1965 Impala become the best-selling single model of all time. A record 1,046,514 units were sold, with roughly 23% being SS variants. Impala SS examples from this generation still attract a lot of attention online.

The top engine for the non-SS 1965 Impala was the familiar Turbo-Fire 409-cubic-inch V8, making 400 horsepower. For the SS, Chevy also offered the L78 V8, a 396-cubic-inch V8 rated at 425 gross horsepower. A year later, the L72 427-cubic-inch V8 joined the options list, also rated for up to 425 hp. The powerplant featured a forged crankshaft and pistons, solid lifters, and a dual exhaust system. The SS 427 continued into 1967 and 1968, but with a slightly different L36 engine, still with 427 cubic inches, but now rated at 385 hp. In 1969, output increased to 390 hp.

Sources indicate that the final Impala SS came with 303 hp, which is the most of any modern generation. The supercharged V6 in the previous eighth-generation SS was replaced with a naturally aspirated 5.3-liter LS4 V8. That results in a zero-to-60 mph dash of 5.6 seconds, which is on par with a modern-day Mazda Miata – but remember, this was 20 years ago.

Sources indicate that that seems straightforward enough, but the final-generation Impala SS has some quirks that don't match its muscle-era badge. Notably, the ninth-generation Impala was front-wheel-drive, and naturally, so was the SS variant. Power traveled through a four-speed automatic transmission, albeit a heavy-duty version. Despite having an upgraded suspension that helped this SS go beyond a rental car-spec version, reviews of the day weren't particularly kind to the SS. In a 2006 road test, Car and Driver stated, "The SS seems to have been created to produce impressive numbers on paper with little regard to driver enjoyment." Nonetheless, the Impala SS's swan song continued through the 2009 model year.

After a quarter-century hiatus, Chevrolet resurrected the Impala SS for the 1994 model year. This time, it was packaged in a rear-wheel-drive sedan with a 260-horsepower 5.7-liter V8 engine under the hood. Engineers didn't have to dig too far into the parts bin. This LT1 V8 already saw duty in the Camaro and Corvette, although there are different LT1 versions over the years. However, the engine in the Impala SS was modified with cast-iron cylinder heads and a different camshaft. It was also tuned for more torque: 330 pound-feet in this application. By today's standards, a 0-to-60 mph dash of seven seconds is nothing exciting, but this was three decades ago, and this Impala SS weighed about 4,300 pounds.

According to recent reports, that bulk came from the full-sized Caprice, which underpinned this seventh-generation version. In effect, you could say that Chevrolet made a civilian version of the Caprice police car. The vehicle included an upgraded suspension, improved cooling, larger disc brakes, and a limited-slip differential. The five-spoke aluminum wheels and subtle strips of exterior chrome trim helped distinguish this Impala from its workhorse siblings. Leather upholstery was another clue. For its final production year, 1996, the column-mounted shifter was moved to the center console, and a tachometer was added. That's why low-mileage 1996 Impala SS examples still hold strong collector appeal.

Industry observers note that the short-lived eighth-generation Impala SS (2004–2005) stands out for a couple of reasons besides having the lowest engine output (240 horsepower). Namely, it's the only Impala SS with a V6 engine. Yet this is no ordinary six-cylinder powerplant; it's General Motors' 3.8-liter Series II engine with an Eaton supercharger, known for its broad torque band.

In a recent development, this Impala SS is based on the eighth-generation Impala, which was introduced for the 2000 model year as a front-wheel-drive sedan. Fast forward to 2004, and Chevrolet added the SS variant to the lineup, marking the first Impala SS that spins the front wheels. An upgraded four-speed automatic transmission controls the setup, but this Chevy also has larger anti-roll bars, modified springs, and Goodyear performance tires. As a result, 0-60 mph came in 6.5 seconds.

To go beyond a plain-Jane Impala, the automaker also added four round taillights (marketing language called this a Corvette-inspired treatment), black-only exterior paint, a small rear spoiler, leather upholstery, and a slathering of SS badges inside and out. This Impala was axed after 2005 to make way for the aforementioned 2006 Impala SS with a more powerful V8 engine.
