#45. 5 Four-Cylinder Engines With Terrible Reputations For Reliability

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1794 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik

5 Four-Cylinder Engines With Terrible Reputations For Reliability

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1794 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that four-cylinder engines come with their own set of pros and cons, just like six-, eight-, ten-, and even twelve-cylinder designs.
  • In addition, engine development has grown increasingly complex in the modern age.
  • Every engine contains components that eventually wear out, and the line between an expected maintenance item and a genuine engineering or manufacturing defect can sometimes be hard to draw.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that four-cylinder engines come with their own set of pros and cons, just like six-, eight-, ten-, and even twelve-cylinder designs. Today, four-cylinder engines are the workhorses of the industry, powering everything from inexpensive daily drivers to luxury cars and high-performance models. Their appeal lies largely in a balance of efficiency, packaging, performance, and cost — but that same appeal means they're built in enormous numbers and pushed through a huge range of operating conditions.

In addition, engine development has grown increasingly complex in the modern age. Forced induction, hybrid systems, and sophisticated electronics have all added layers of engineering that simply didn't exist to the same degree a generation ago. But even without these factors, designing an engine capable of running flawlessly for decades is an extraordinarily difficult task.

Every engine contains components that eventually wear out, and the line between an expected maintenance item and a genuine engineering or manufacturing defect can sometimes be hard to draw. In other cases, though, the problem is impossible to ignore. Excessive oil consumption, failed head gaskets, damaged bearings, overheating, and catastrophic internal failures can turn an otherwise promising engine into one owners learn to avoid.

Because the engine is the heart of any vehicle, major failures can promptly damage the reputation of both the powertrain and the manufacturer that built it. And since four-cylinders are generally known for their reliability, the bad ones stand out even more. That's why some four-cylinder engines have become especially notorious for recurring defects, expensive repairs, and widespread owner complaints. Here are our picks of the five biggest offenders.

According to recent reports, one Theta II engine problem from Hyundai and Kia is a prime example of the worst things that can go wrong. In 2015, Hyundai recalled (15V-568) around 470,000 units of the 2011/2012 Sonata equipped with either the 2.0-liter or the 2.4-liter Theta II inline-4 engine. Hyundai built the affected engines at its Alabama plant, where machining work on the engine's crankshaft left metal debris behind.

Recent findings suggest that NHTSA's filing ties that debris to potential connecting rod bearing failure, and lists a knocking sound or an illuminated CEL as the warning signs before the engine dies. To say the least, customers didn't take that well since it led to an approval of a massive $1.3 billion settlement. For example, on CarComplaints, the 2016 Sonata's engine complaints carry a severity rating of "Really Awful," with an average failure mileage of just 24,456 miles and more than 1,000 complaints filed against the engine alone.

According to recent reports, on the same site, the 2011 Sonata's seized engine ranks as the No. 1 Sonata engine problem, costing an average of $5,100 to fix at around 96,000 miles. J.D. Power's 2014 Vehicle Dependability Study, which surveyed owners of three-year-old 2011 models, also placed Hyundai among the bottom five brands, with a disappointing 169 problems per 100 vehicles, on average. Separately from the civil settlement, NHTSA announced consent orders against both Kia and Hyundai in 2020, penalizing them a combined $210 million.

These penalties followed an NHTSA review that concluded the recall covering the 1.6 million-plus Theta II vehicles had come too late, compounded by paperwork Hyundai and Kia filed with the agency that didn't hold up. This engine's reputation is so severe that enthusiasts on Reddit point to the Theta inline-4s as among the least reliable engines, and we even included it in our list of the worst engines of all time.

Do you know what's worse for an engine than metal shavings? Fire. This is exactly what plagued Ford's 1.6-liter EcoBoost. NHTSA's 2012 filing for a recall (12V-336) covered roughly 9,320 Escapes with an engine compartment fuel line that may have been damaged during assembly. However, that was not enough to fix the problem of engines bursting into flames. Two months later, a separate recall of 6,146 examples was issued (12V-431) over a different issue entirely: escaping antifreeze that could ignite. One would think that this would be it, but it was not. Three months later, another recall (12V-551) expanded the fire recall to more than 80,000 Escapes and Fusions over coolant leaks reaching the hot exhaust system.

Industry observers note that by November 2013, Ford issued two more recalls on the same day. One (13V-583) covered 139,917 Escapes for yet another failure mode: overheating cracking the cylinder head and letting oil find its way out onto hot surfaces. The other (13V-584) covered the same vehicles from the original 12V-336 recall, because the replacement fuel line had, in some cases, been installed incorrectly the first time. Then, in 2017, another recall (17V-209) was issued for fire problems, covering 208,584 vehicles powered by the 1.6-liter.

It is not all about recalls though. The 1.6-liter is also prone to coolant intrusion, which Ford Authority called "very common with EcoBoost four-cylinder powerplants" after its tech found it in a 1.6-liter 2014 Escape. Plenty of owners on forums are dissatisfied, too, with one Bronco Sport Forum member echoing that "it's not a matter of IF but WHEN you will get coolant intrusion and have to do major engine work." Ford, it seems, is back at it with problems – five Ford models were just recalled for an EcoBoost engine problem, this time over faulty piston manufacturing in the 1.5-liter and 2.3-liter units.

Sources indicate that the 2017 Nissan's VC-Turbo was the world's first production engine capable of adjusting its own compression ratio on the fly, but its positive reputation crumbled soon after. In June 2025, Nissan filed the first recall tied to the VC-Turbo family. 25V-437 covered 443,899 Rogues, Altimas, and Infiniti models, spanning both the 1.5-liter three-cylinder and 2.0-liter four-cylinder versions of the engine, over bearings that can fail outright.

That wasn't the end. Eight months later, in February 2026, Nissan filed two more recalls. The first one (26V-080) covered 323,917 Rogues and pinned the blame on heat and the oil itself degrading under high running temperatures. NHTSA's filing warns the consequences can go beyond a stalled engine, noting "a bearing failure may cause a breach in the engine block, allowing hot oil to be discharged, increasing the risk of an engine fire." The second recall (26V-081) covered 318,781 Rogues for a gear inside the electronic throttle body that can fracture during startup. Across the three campaigns, Nissan has recalled more than a million VC-Turbo vehicles, though the two 2026 recalls overlap with some vehicles already covered by the 2025 campaign.

Owners have also complained about the VC-Turbo. One 2022 Rogue owner wrote on CarComplaints, where the VC-Turbo is rated "Pretty Bad," said that the dealer told them, "The engine is completely shot and needs to be replaced. Total cost $14000." Enthusiasts have soured on it as well over the years. According to Endurance Warranty, mechanics warn about ticking or knocking noises, which could indicate worn bearings and cost more than $5,000 in out-of-warranty repairs for VC-Turbo-equipped Rogues and Altimas.

We've previously covered Nissan's reliability, citing Consumer Reports, pointing to "ongoing complications with the clever but problematic variable-compression VC-Turbo engine" as one of the factors pushing Nissan down to eighth place among the most reliable used-car brands.

Recent findings suggest that the hybrid Jeep 2.0-liter turbo-four didn't fail because of a design flaw; it failed because sand does not mix well with engine internals. NHTSA's filing for the November 2025 recall (25V-766) covered 112,859 of these PHEV SUVs after Chrysler identified a supplier quality lapse: the debris from the engine-block sand-casting process was never fully removed before the blocks went into production.

Left inside, that sand works its way through the engine and can eventually cause a fire or a dead engine. Chrysler didn't have a fix at the time of the recall and only started offering software updates and, where needed, engine block replacements in May 2026. These same 4xe hybrids had already been recalled once before over a separate battery fire risk.

Chrysler's 2.0-liter PHEV has stumbled before that, too. A 2022 recall (22V-865) included 62,909 Wrangler 4xe models over the engine just shutting down. The vehicle's own diagnostics can misread a communication fault and decide to just power off the vehicle while driving. This has led to two accidents and one injury. RepairPal also ranks the Wrangler 25th out of 26 compact SUVs when it comes to reliability, though that rating covers the whole lineup, not just the 4xe.

What's even worse is that the same problem resurfaced three years later, this time in the Grand Cherokee. The September 2025 recall (25V-576) covered 91,787 more PHEVs after Chrysler traced another defect to the hybrid control processor, which is a very similar problem description to the 2022 recall, just on a different model. One JL Wrangler Forums member noted oil dilution had their 4xe asking for an oil change after under 310 miles. And if the engine goes bang, one owner got quoted $7,500 for a replacement 2.0T from the dealer.

Sources indicate that back in 1971, Chevy rushed the Vega's development into just 24 months to hit a deadline set by GM president Ed Cole. To save weight, engineers skipped the cylinder sleeves that a block like this would normally need. Instead, they bet on a hardened Reynolds Aluminum alloy carrying enough silicon to serve as the bore surface on its own, bolted to a conventional cast-iron head. It held up under normal use, but severe heat degraded that silicon content, and the pistons would then scuff against the weakened bore walls.

Aluminum and iron don't handle heat the same way, either, and that mismatch is what finally cracked the head gasket. Chevrolet made the problem worse — early Vegas shipped with a radiator too small for the engine's needs and no way to recover coolant once lost. Cracking valve stem seals let oil into the cylinders too, and since oil also carries heat away from the engine, that only makes overheating worse.

The car's other systems fared no better. In April 1972, Chevrolet recalled roughly 129,000 Vegas (72V075000) after backfires ruptured the muffler and ignited leaking gasoline. Less than two months later, another recall (72V112000) covered 350,000 more Vegas whose idle-stop solenoid bracket could jam the throttle open. Enthusiasts were also very critical, as one Ford-Trucks forum member described the original Vega in a thread on the worst GM engines: "You didn't change the oil every 3,000 miles. You replaced the block.".

By 1974, overheating had become bad enough that Chevy notified 1.3 million owners it would cover damage under warranty. A real fix didn't come until 1976's "Dura-Built 140" engine — fresh long-life valve stem seals, and hydraulic valve lifters, a beefed-up head gasket, and new cooling passages for the engine. Chevy even covered it with a massive five-year/60,000-mile warranty.

#43. 7 Fuel Sipping Classic Cars For Thrifty Driving Enthusiasts

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2098 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik

7 Fuel Sipping Classic Cars For Thrifty Driving Enthusiasts

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2098 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that it might seem anachronistic to chase fuel economy when you're hunting for a classic car.
  • Plus you've got a pocket humblebrag at the ready wherever you cruise in your fuel-sipping steed.
  • Recent findings suggest that even if you're not solely chasing fuel economy, you can be frugal and have fun simultaneously.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that it might seem anachronistic to chase fuel economy when you're hunting for a classic car. But it's not absurd to want an affordable classic if that's all your wallet can muster. And in that case, it's probably also true that you're hardly itching to shell out for a massive weekly thrashing at the pump. After all, however you define a classic, they tend to be parts-and-labor-costs hungry. At the time of this writing, AAA notes the national average for a gallon of gas sits at $4.12, up 36% versus a year ago, when it was $3.04. And in California a gallon of regular will run you $5.87. Ouch.

Plus you've got a pocket humblebrag at the ready wherever you cruise in your fuel-sipping steed. Imagine showing up at a cars and coffee with your vintage ride and telling the assembled dudes (always, always, dudes) that your 1990 Honda CRX gets a combined 40-ish mpg  – which torches the fuel economy of most modern cars.

Recent findings suggest that even if you're not solely chasing fuel economy, you can be frugal and have fun simultaneously. Take, for instance, a merely 23-year-old Mini Cooper S. It gets 31 mpg on the highway and its supercharged 1.6-liter engine can tug you to 60 mph in 6.9 seconds. That's not too shabby for a car that Hagerty valuation puts at somewhere between $8,000 and $11,000. It's pretty tough to name another used city ripper that lean on gas and as entertaining to drive.

It has been revealed that well, actually, I'll try. Since the whole reason for this game is to induce debate among Jalopnik readers who live to lambaste our dumb lists.

It has been revealed that the Honda CRX, according to Hagerty, has skyrocketed in value, up over 113% in the past three years. Now you'll pay at least $14,000 for one. That mentioned, what soulless used car might you get instead for that kind of money?

Plus, the CRX (in the HF "High Fuel" version) delivered up to 47 mpg! Even models with reasonably higher output, like the 91-horsepower 1.5Si, breached the 30 mpg mark. Possibly the reason the CRX has risen in collectors' eyes has to do with the simple idea that a car that weighs less than 2,000 pounds doesn't need more than 91 horsepower. And in the guise of the 1.5Si, a contemporary review in Car & Driver found the sport suspension ideal for twisty corners, and at 1,840 pounds, 91 horsepower was more than adequate. Yeah, every CRX should have featured two engines, but I'm guessing that'd be bad for fuel economy and the concept of this list.

If you're hunting, from 1988 onward the CRX got four-wheel double-wishbone suspension and ditched the less advanced torsion-bar front and beam-axle rear of older CRXs. By 1990, Honda had added four-wheel disc brakes to the Si grade.

These lithe two-doors feature a funky non-second row, with a bench behind the front seats that can be flipped down to yield a reasonably capacious hatch space. That makes the CRX a more pragmatic sporty car than, say, the Fiat X 1/9 on this list.

If you're pursuing a classic that's fuel-sipping, you probably don't want to spend a fortune to acquire it. That's kind of defeating the point. Toyota's mid-engine MR2, which we got in many guises in the U.S. from 1985 through the early 2000s, has a strong following. Maybe too strong. Hagerty says turbocharged 200-horsepower W20s — the second-generation MR2 with softer shoulders and a longer wheelbase — run between $23,000 and nearly $39,000.

According to recent reports, okay, those are faster. But at that price they're blowing a huge hole in this story's premise. Of course, the reason you want one is the same reason you might lust after the Fiat X 1/9 on this list. When they're properly engineered, mid-engine cars can offer magical balance through corners; Hagerty called this first generation, the W10, "flickable.".

In a recent development, that's the joy you're after, and you can also still afford the W10, which averages from $10,300 to $18,000 per Hagerty. These were only good for 112 hp from a tiny 1.6-liter inline-4. But that still meant you could gallop to 60 mph in 8.2 seconds according to Car & Driver — and that version of the MR2 achieved 27 mpg in the city.

Recent findings suggest that want more oomph? One route is the middle-ground supercharged W10 MR2, which won't hurt you too much at the pump, delivering 23 mpg city and 28 highway. Output jumped to 145 hp, resulting in a 6.5-second 0-60 sprint. Hagerty notes these range between $15,800 and $26,200, which isn't that harsh a price penalty, and still cheaper than later W20s.

According to recent reports, not that you need my two cents, since scads of automotive journalists have owned or currently own 1990s MX-5 Miatas, but in my experience this car absolutely fits the remit of both frugality and fun. Also, I stand firmly with the crowd that says everyone should drive a Miata at least once. I frequently loathe the fact I sold mine. It was a trouble-free grin machine.

According to recent reports, okay, they're slow, too. With a 116-hp 1.6-liter inline-4 you're not going to win many stoplight wars. But that's not what matters. The early 1990s MX-5 Miata, at 155 inches long (a scant 13 feet), is nearly 2 feet shorter than a current Porsche 911 Carrera. Pint-sized and low in weight — barely 2,200 pounds — makes carving around corners gloriously entertaining. To me, the Miata is one of very few cars that's fantastically entertaining even when you're driving slower than the speed limit.

Hagerty indicates finding a Miata from the early 1990s ought to run you between about $7,000 and $12,200, and with a combined fuel economy of 24 mpg, these little five-speeds are reasonably economical to operate, if not exactly trying to swipe that Honda CRX's crown. Miatas are also considered highly reliable, which is another measure of thrift. And that's in contrast to the British two-seat sports cars of the 1960s and 1970s they were designed to copy.

Industry observers note that the 1979 Fiat X 1/9 is neither as logical as the Honda CRX nor as practical. It's here because it achieved 26 mpg city fuel economy and because we think the "driving enthusiasts" of our headline find going around corners more fun than bombing straight ahead.

Besides, with only 67 horsepower from its 1.5-liter engine, the Fiat X 1/9 wasn't designed with the quarter mile in mind. Instead, with its mid-engine, rear-wheel-drive setup, the Fiat puts all its mass (plus, you, the driver) in the middle of the machine. Car & Driver argued that made the Fiat a blast for scorching around corners, and yet kind enough to less seasoned drivers. Meaning, it loses grip progressively, rather than suddenly, so it's less likely to cause you physical harm.

The magazine also found that it took nearly 12 seconds to journey to 60 mph, so if you're hurt behind the wheel of the  X 1/9, it might be because other drivers have grown impatient in your wake. Then again, just let them pass! You're cruising under sunshine thanks to the Fiat's removable lightweight lid that can be stowed promptly in the front trunk.

This Fiat is definitely emblematic of la dolce vita. Also, it's a pretty affordable, sweet way to motor, since Hagerty ballparks a 1979 X 1/9 between $8,600 and $14,000. That's not the $7,115 Car & Driver said this model cost when tested. But adjusted for inflation, that 1979 cash would be worth $35,100 today, so your $8,600 X 1/9 is a dang bargain.

Acura Integras from the late 1990s are no longer sleepers. Hagerty puts the high end of the 1997 Acura Integra Type R at north of $50,000. Is that expensive or cheap? The brand-new 320-horsepower Integra Type S costs about that much. Keeping budget constraints top of mind here, the Type R is a no-go. But the still-quick Integra GS-R averages more like $10,000 to $20,000 if you eyeball recent sales on Bring a Trailer. For instance, in September 2026, a 2000 Integra GS-R sold there for $20,750.

That's still a car that brings the noise to the tune of 170 hp and an 8,100 rpm redline. My dad had one and I adored that car; he gave me the family Toyota Tercel instead. Woot.

Sources indicate that putting my nostalgia aside, a 1994 Car & Driver shootout of hot hatches awarded the GS-R its top prize in large part for its blend of motorcycle-like revs, excellent five-speed gearbox, and the car's predictable, capable, rewarding handling. Also, its 1.8-liter inline-4 is loud as hell when you're deep in the throttle, which makes the Integra seem properly exotic. Yet, drive it sanely and it's hardly deafening.

Industry observers note that is the Integra the most economical car here? Hardly. Its combined fuel economy of 24 mpg is just decent. Still, you're getting a hatchback that's cheaper on gas than lots of vintage muscle iron, and if you can find one around $20,000 you'll be spending less than the price of any upcoming sports car. You might also care that the Integra even has a functional backseat and decent luggage space.

According to recent reports, by 1989, Mercedes-Benz was making very hot versions of the 190, which began production in 1982. For instance, a 1989 Mercedes-Benz 190E 2.5-16 Evolution, one of only 502 produced, was bid up to nearly $100,000 on Bring a Trailer this spring. Neat. But that hardly fits the mandate of frugality.

Sources indicate that the W120/190 series Benz you probably want would be the modest 72-horsepower 2.2-liter mid-1980s diesel, if in fact your goal is long-wearing life and relatively strong 30 mpg combined fuel economy. Oh, and also unlike a Cosworth-hotted-up 190 that's ticking boxes for collectors capable of throwing down 100 grand, Hagerty puts the price of a used 190D with a base 2.2-liter diesel at as cheap as $3,500.

You could spend a little more and get a modest power bump to the later 1980s 2.5-liter diesel with 93 horsepower, which still delivers 28 mpg combined, and Hagerty notes will cost you between $4,067 and $7,367. Again, name any modern car you can find for so little money.

Industry observers note that all right, I know this is the least enthusiast-focused car in this compilation. But Mercedes gifted the 190 with a five-link rear suspension and gas-filled struts up front, and that yielded if not a purely sporty vibe, a very confident, modern and comfortable ride. You're buying one because they're cheap to acquire, drink diesel slowly, and like a lot of vintage Benzes, are solid as tanks.

Recent findings suggest that last year we told you the 2025 Mini Cooper S 4 Door is like a half-trained puppy you love with all your heart. The thing is, that car's 2026 base price (even without optional paddle shifters) is $34,150 including destination. And there's no option to get a stick-shift version. You may argue that it's a fresh car, and with 201 horsepower will walk all over a 20-year-old version of the supercharged Mini Cooper S. Sure thing. But that 168-hp supercharged 1.5-liter inline 4 had more character than the turbocharged 2.0-liter in the new car.

No, that didn't make it quick. Its 0-60 mph times ran about 6.9 seconds, while the newly introduced one takes 6.3 seconds. Seriously, do you want to pay nearly $30,000 more for a new Mini Cooper S that's less than a second faster to 60 mph, when a 2005 just sold for $4,000 on Bring a Trailer?

There's a Cooper S in my extended family, so I get to drive one pretty regularly. It needs some work. All old cars do. But this one has north of 200,000 miles and it's still ripping around. Just remember to find one with the fun six-speed when you look for your O.G. Mini Cooper S R53, and avoid the version with the continuously variable automatic transmission. Our Mini Cooper burns a little oil, roughly half a quart every three months, which isn't a big deal, and the EPA combined average fuel economy of 25 mpg is spot on.

Today, this counts as a small car, but it's massive enough to be useful, with flip-down rear seats and enough gumption to keep up on the interstate. Fun, frugal, and just old enough to have loads of character? Check, check, and check.

#41. No Car's Lines Were Ruined More Thoroughly Than When The Avanti Was Made Into A Sedan

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (884 w)
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik

No Car's Lines Were Ruined More Thoroughly Than When The Avanti Was Made Into A Sedan

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (884 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Franco-American industrial designer Raymond Loewy's work is infallible, and his four-wheeled designs at Studebaker remain among the most unconventionally beautiful shapes in automotive history.
  • According to recent reports, with company president Sherwood Egbert taking the reins in 1961 and eager to make an impression, he gave Loewy just six weeks to design the now-iconic high-performance halo car for the brand.
  • Unfortunately, while the Avanti was an incredible machine, it wasn't good enough to save a floundering Studebaker from collapse.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Franco-American industrial designer Raymond Loewy's work is infallible, and his four-wheeled designs at Studebaker remain among the most unconventionally beautiful shapes in automotive history. The original Avanti was not only one of the coolest cars of its era, but it also once held the record for fastest production car on the market. The Avanti was famous for delivering serious world-beating performance to the American market years before the Big Three went hog wild in the heady muscle car days of the late 1960s.

According to recent reports, with company president Sherwood Egbert taking the reins in 1961 and eager to make an impression, he gave Loewy just six weeks to design the now-iconic high-performance halo car for the brand. Egbert's philosophical demand for the Avanti was that it "must be tops in speed, braking, handling, safety features, and general innovation—and please don't spend any money." A 170-mile-per-hour fiberglass-bodied V8-powered luxury coupe that could take on the Corvette and Thunderbird without flinching, the Avanti was all that and more.

Unfortunately, while the Avanti was an incredible machine, it wasn't good enough to save a floundering Studebaker from collapse. Studebaker's went bust just four years later, and a crew of enterprising former Studebaker dealers, brothers Arnold and Nate Altman, and Leo Newman, joined forces to purchase the Avanti name, tooling, and plant space. From there, they spun up the Avanti name into its own brand.

While it was initially a great thing that a revolutionary car like the Avanti was able to live on in the world after its manufacturer's demise (much like its Excalibur cousin), what happened to it over time is a criminal act of automotive aesthetic. While the Avanti lived on through 2006, what happened in 1989 should be remembered as the tragedy it was.

Sources indicate that in 1965, as the Studebaker parts began to run out, the Altman/Newman Avanti was modified to accept Chevrolet small-block power, buying in 327 cubic-inch Corvette engines with 300 ponies. Thus the Avanti II was born. Avanti continued with GM engines through the 1980s, with power waning following the fuel crisis-riddled 1970s, until it received a tepid 305 cu in. mill making just 155 horses turned through a three-speed automatic.

Sources indicate that when Nate Altman passed away in the late 1970s, his brother began a blueprint to sell what remained of Avanti Motors Corporation, and in 1982, real estate developer Stephen H. Blake bought Avanti. It took until 1985 for the original run of Studebaker chassis to run out, and Blake had the car re-designed to accommodate new underpinnings. According to a period Popular Mechanics article, Blake hired former Pontiac engineer Herb Adams to develop a more exciting Avanti platform: "With backbone construction, a torque tube, and '85 Corvette aluminum IRS rear end, the chassis is expected to be hundreds of pounds lighter than the present framework." Sadly, this plan was scrapped as it was too expensive, and the Avanti moved to a Monte Carlo chassis instead. By 1987, the company was bankrupt and sold once again.

Industry observers note that the organization passed through the hands of Michael Kelly before John Cafaro bought the remnants and moved it from South Bend, Indiana, to his Youngstown, Ohio, home. Around the same time, GM ended the G-body Monte Carlo, and Avanti was again left without a supply of underpinnings. The car was re-tooled again for the much longer B-body Caprice. While the chassis was shortened under the Avanti coupe and convertible, Cafaro kept it at full length for a upcoming sedan body style for 1989.

Have you ever noticed that a limousine never looks quite right? Car designers don't typically craft vehicle shapes with the intent of cutting them in half, extending the middle several feet, and grafting them back together. The result is an uncanny, almost haphazard aesthetic. While unorthodox in its shape, the Avanti was an interesting looking car in its original Loewy shape. By the 1980s, it had been prodded and pulled, the petite chrome bumpers replaced by gaudy molded fiberglass, the round headlights swapped for then-popular rectangular sealed beams. It had become an amalgam of old and upcoming, with European luxury-inspired touches juxtaposed with hot rodder tchotchke, none of it good. Then came the sedan, a true stylistic abomination.

The 1989-only Avanti Sedan proved immediately undesirable and was ditched for 1990. As it turned out, there was already a very tiny sliver of the car market interested in an Avanti in the first place, and they definitely didn't want an uglier one. Especially as it was effectively little more than a heavy and anemic Chevrolet Caprice underneath. The extreme hand-built price premium wasn't worth paying. Thankfully for the world, just 90 examples of the Avanti Sedan were built, as unprofitable as it was unpopular. Cafaro's attempt at reviving Avanti had failed. The factory sat idle, full of half-finished cars, until 1999.

Kelly re-purchased the organization and planned a massive revival of the brand with Ford Mustang powertrains, moving the whole mess to Villa Rica, Georgia (and later Cancun, Mexico), but he was arrested in 2006 on fraud charges, and Avanti was disbanded once more. What once was the most advanced American car on the market, it seems, was doomed to an ignominious fate of slow collapse and mis-management.

Tech Report: Check your ego at the door: Stellantis’ new electric dolly turns ANY car into a tow rig

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We all know the type: grizzled stubble, wraparound PitVipers, a MAGA hat quietly retired after last week’s deep-blue shellacking, and a pristine, polished pickup parked in the driveway that they “need for towing.” With Stellantis’ upcoming patent for an AI-powered electric tow dolly that turns just about ANY vehicle into a capable tow rig, however, those might need a new to find a new excuse to keep that gas-guzzler.
  • It has been revealed that originally filed in 2023, Stellantis received US Patent No.
  • In other words, the dolly takes on many of the jobs that traditionally require a big tow vehicle: providing the pulling power, managing the trailer’s weight and controlling its braking and traction.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We all know the type: grizzled stubble, wraparound PitVipers, a MAGA hat quietly retired after last week’s deep-blue shellacking, and a pristine, polished pickup parked in the driveway that they “need for towing.” With Stellantis’ upcoming patent for an AI-powered electric tow dolly that turns just about ANY vehicle into a capable tow rig, however, those might need a new to find a new excuse to keep that gas-guzzler.

It has been revealed that originally filed in 2023, Stellantis received US Patent No. 12,779,916 for its electric tow dolly on 03NOV2026. The patent covers a machine that’s designed to shoulder the trailer’s hitch load with its own ball hitch or fifth-wheel plate, using an on-board electric motor and battery to get the trailer going while its regenerative braking system and AI-backed steering and traction control system keeps everything pointed in the right direction.

In other words, the dolly takes on many of the jobs that traditionally require a big tow vehicle: providing the pulling power, managing the trailer’s weight and controlling its braking and traction. The vehicle up front doesn’t necessarily need a massive motor, heavy-duty suspension or oversized brakes. With a system like this, you could argue that the “tow vehicle” isn’t really a tow vehicle at all. It’s more of a “lead vehicle,” since the dolly is the one doing the towing … and it can follow just about anything – including the diminutive (and supremely affordable) Fiat 500e, which is also made by Stellantis.

To be clear, this isn’t just Uncle Jojo making fun of the commuter conveys – Stellantis’ patent describes the dolly as being equipped with an autonomous control system using cameras, sensors, a controller, and an advanced, four wheel steer-by-wire system. It also specifically discusses how the dolly’s independently powered acceleration, braking and steering, and sway controls essentially remove the need to own a truck in the first place.

The dolly system’s truck bed sides and small size allow people to experience the functionality and utility of a truck only when they need it, allowing them to own a smaller, cheaper, and more fuel efficient vehicle that suits daily use needs.

There are some pretty obvious practical questions still to answer, of course, including how much battery capacity the dolly would need, how much weight it could handle and how it would perform on long grades or in emergency braking situations. And, to be clear, a patent isn’t a product announcement or proof that Stellantis plans to put one of these things on sale – heck, if I were Stellantis’ CEO, I’d patent this thing just to prevent anyone else from building one so I could keep selling ancient, low-tech, high-margin Ram Trucks – but it’s a neat idea.

That is a funny picture with the tiny 500e "pulling" that huge trailer.

Industry observers note that but on a more serious note, there's so much that goes into pulling. It's control. It's stopping. It's being smart enough to watch the weather forecast and know when to pull off the road and sit out a storm.

The irony here? Back in 2004, I began working at a dealership selling Chrysler, Dodge, Ram and Jeep. So of course we had the big trucks and many came in buying the 2500/3500 with the Cummins Diesel. Chrysler Corp made every sales person go through specialized training for the trucks and towing. Every sale had to include a form signed by the customer about towing and the limits of the truck they were buying. Hidden in there was a clause that stated the customer would NOT use the truck to tow more than the listed (legal) amount. If the customer didn't sign it, we were told by Chrysler that would be a no sale. They were very serious, and for good reason.

I may not like seeing all these huge trucks on the road. But when it comes to towing, mass is your friend. A powerful engine, huge (good) brakes and a well trained driver are a must.

According to recent reports, I think it’s neat, anyway. What do you guys think? Are you ready to trade in your massive-battery Chevy Silverado EV or Volvo VNR 800 on a new Topolino, or are you going to keep driving inefficient 99% of the time? Let us know, in the comments.

#38. What The US Midterm Elections Mean For Climate Progress

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (937 w)

What The US Midterm Elections Mean For Climate Progress

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (937 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cleantechnica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, people across the United States voted in record numbers in last week’s incredibly consequential election, which has completely changed the makeup of Congress for its upcoming term beginning in January 2027.
  • Industry observers note that will the Trump administration acknowledge voters’ repudiation of its destructive agenda and work in cooperation with this upcoming Congress?
  • Recent findings suggest that energy affordability concerns, opposition to proliferating data centers, and anger at corruption and extreme economic inequality were undoubtedly driving forces in how people voted.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, people across the United States voted in record numbers in last week’s incredibly consequential election, which has completely changed the makeup of Congress for its upcoming term beginning in January 2027. The success of our electoral processes—still underway—should not be taken for granted. It’s a win for democracy when millions of citizens peacefully claim their right to a government of, by, and for the people.

Industry observers note that will the Trump administration acknowledge voters’ repudiation of its destructive agenda and work in cooperation with this upcoming Congress? That remains to be seen, and I’m not holding my breath. But there’s no question that the shift in Congress has significant implications for the administration’s ability to continue to ram through its anti-science, authoritarian agenda—including on climate and clean energy challenges.

Recent findings suggest that energy affordability concerns, opposition to proliferating data centers, and anger at corruption and extreme economic inequality were undoubtedly driving forces in how people voted. While not everyone explicitly named climate change as a top glitch (although many did put it in their top three), its fingerprints are all over the concerns a majority of voters did name in polls.

According to recent reports, if you care about addressing the high costs of electricity and gas, then you must reckon with the fact that this current fossil energy crisis, unleashed by the Trump administration’s war against Iran, is an extreme manifestation of the risks of fossil fuel dependence. The benefits of a transition away from fossil fuels to renewable energy—renewable energy that the Trump administration has relentlessly attacked, further driving up costs for consumers—are tremendous. If you are deeply concerned about the rapid, unregulated build-out of data centers, you know that it comes with huge risks for communities related to climate, water, pollution, health, and electricity cost burdens. And it’s so clear that the Trump administration’s corruption, lies about climate science, and massive giveaways to fossil fuel polluters are leaving us all bearing the high costs of climate damages while large corporations and the president’s inner circle are raking in enormous profits.

Here’s another reality: regardless of politics, climate change is here, and science shows it’s rapidly worsening with the world’s imminent overshoot of 1.5°C of global warming. Communities are already experiencing deadly and costly climate impacts, including extreme heatwaves, catastrophic wildfires, record-breaking flooding, drought, accelerating sea level rise, intense ocean heat, irreversible loss of glaciers and ice sheets, stresses to critical ecosystems and more. These impacts are showing up in people’s daily lives—harming their health, destroying homes, livelihoods, and critical infrastructure, raising insurance premiums, hammering businesses, stressing water supplies, and threatening food security and affordability.

Climate change and clean energy are pocketbook issues. They are a lot more than that, of course. And climate change does not care if you live in a red state or a blue state. (One can ask if that is that even a relevant frame after an election that scrambled all conventional wisdom about “red” and “blue” dichotomies.).

Importantly, we will soon have a Congress where a majority accepts the scientific evidence on climate change. (Yes, I also wish we could take that for granted in 2026, but not in US politics, sadly.) That’s an important start and means we can advocate for policymakers to legislate based on the facts, instead of being stuck fighting disinformation and lies.

Here’s what this seismic “change election” could mean for action on climate change, some cautions about what likely won’t change right away, and what we’ll have to keep fighting for.

According to recent reports, we will have to keep fighting back in courts to hold the Trump administration accountable for egregiously flouting the law. We’ve already had a major win in a lawsuit where the administration was found to be violating the Federal Advisory Committee Act in secretly setting up a ‘Climate Working Group’ stacked with climate contrarians to draft a sham science report, which the EPA then used to justify its proposal to gut the Endangerment Finding. We’ve also filed suit against the administration for repealing the Endangerment Finding, contrary to law, science, and the public interest.

On the international front, the Trump administration has shamefully exited the bedrock UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement, and that won’t change as long as it is in power. As I write from COP31 in Türkiye, the administration’s abandonment of global climate cooperation is very much on my mind; it’s crucial for the rest of the world to forge ahead regardless of the high stakes. There is a real risk that a beleaguered Trump administration will double down on its authoritarian ways and continue to find new ways to disrupt global climate progress and multilateral institutions. But Congress now has the power and responsibility to keep this reckless administration in check and ensure it is held accountable, at home and on the global stage.

“Change elections” come weighted with the hopes and dreams of many. As climate justice advocates, we know that policymakers have pushed off meaningful climate action far too long, and those failures are putting us all at profound risk. Yet, deep-pocketed fossil fuel interests, Massive Tech, and other powerful entities continue to obstruct and delay action, still hold all too much sway over both parties in Congress, and we can expect their harmful tactics to ratchet up. So now it’s our responsibility to fight for what comes next, to make our shared dreams come true. Because those dreams of a safer, more just world for generations of young people to come must become reality.

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (870 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Jalopnik

Industry News: Honda Did Make Diesel Engines, Here's Why They Disappeared

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (870 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that we all know and love Honda for its high-revving gasoline engines (remember the S600's 9,500-rpm motor?) and, more recently, its frugal hybrid powertrains.
  • Interestingly, Honda's former senior chief engineer, Kenichi Nagahiro, was far from a fan of diesel engines due to their noise and smell.
  • In a recent development, honda also introduced diesel engines for the Indian market back in 2013, giving buyers a more fuel-efficient alternative in models such as the Amaze and City.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that we all know and love Honda for its high-revving gasoline engines (remember the S600's 9,500-rpm motor?) and, more recently, its frugal hybrid powertrains. However, the Japanese automaker's legacy isn't just built on gasoline, as it used to offer a family of diesel engines that powered popular cars like the Civic, Accord, CR-V, and City.

Interestingly, Honda's former senior chief engineer, Kenichi Nagahiro, was far from a fan of diesel engines due to their noise and smell. But diesel was booming in Europe in the early 2000s, so Nagahiro locked in and built Honda's first in-house diesel engine — the 2.2-liter i-CTDi. And since Nagahiro hated diesel engines in their then-current forms, he ensured the 2.2-liter i-CTDi would live up to his standards.

In a recent development, honda also introduced diesel engines for the Indian market back in 2013, giving buyers a more fuel-efficient alternative in models such as the Amaze and City. However, that changed over the following decade as emissions regulations became stricter and customer preferences shifted toward gasoline and hybrid vehicles. Honda began phasing out diesel models in Europe in 2019, with the withdrawal completed by 2021. In India, Honda continued selling diesel cars for longer but ended production in early 2023. By then, India was the last place Honda still built diesel engines, including those for CR-Vs sold in Thailand and the Philippines. These decisions were not down to any single problem, and certainly not reliability (after all, diesel engines generally last longer than their gas counterparts). Instead, they were a consequence of the growing cost of keeping these engines compliant with tightening emissions regulations, declining demand, and Honda's changing powertrain strategy.

The 2.2-liter four-cylinder i-CTDi debuted in 2003 and appeared in European-market versions of the Accord and, later, the Civic, CR-V, and FR-V. The 2.2-liter i-CTDi was compliant with Euro 4 emissions regulations, had a rated mileage of 43.5 mpg on Europe's official test cycle (52.3 mpg in imperial gallons), and produced 138 hp and 251 lb-ft of torque. In 2007, Honda introduced an updated Euro-5-compliant version of the engine, dubbed the 2.2-liter i-DTEC, which also powered the Accord, Civic, and CR-V in several markets. The engine developed 147 to 178 hp and 258 to 280 lb-ft of torque.

Recent findings suggest that in 2012, Honda introduced its smaller 1.6-liter four-cylinder i-DTEC, part of its "Earth Dreams" line of engines. The 1.6-liter i-DTEC was over 100 pounds lighter and more fuel-efficient (65.4 mpg in the Civic; 78.5 in imperial gallons) than the 2.2-liter i-DTEC, and attracted lower taxes in Europe because it dipped below the 100-gram-per-kilometer mark for carbon dioxide emissions. In Europe, the 1.6-liter i-DTEC found its way under the hoods of the Civic, CR-V, and HR-V. It was also used in the Civic and CR-V sold in India, with the latter also available in Thailand and the Philippines. Output ranged from 118 to 158 hp and 221 to 258 lb-ft of torque.

Then came the 1.5-liter four-cylinder i-DTEC in 2013 — Honda's final in-house diesel engine. Developed specifically for India, the 1.5-liter i-DTEC was essentially a downsized variant of the 1.6-liter i-DTEC engine, and made its debut in the first-generation Amaze. Honda subsequently offered the 1.5-liter i-DTEC in the India-spec City, Mobilio, Jazz, BR-V, and WR-V. The engine developed 100 hp and 148 lb-ft of torque, and was rated for staggeringly good fuel efficiency of up to 64.4 mpg on India's official test cycle (27.4 km/l).

The main reason Honda abandoned diesel cars was the increasingly difficult economics of keeping them compliant with tougher emissions regulations, especially in light of decreasing global demand. In Europe, the aftermath of Volkswagen's Dieselgate emissions scandal invited greater scrutiny of diesel cars, while stricter Euro 6 requirements and real-world emissions testing increased the engineering burden on automakers. Compared to gasoline engines, diesels generally require more elaborate exhaust after-treatment systems to control emissions. Updating these systems, validating them, and certifying them for different models adds development and production costs. Honda unveiled in 2019 that it would phase out diesel cars in Europe by 2021 as it shifted toward electrified vehicles.

Industry observers note that india presented a similar challenge. The introduction of Bharat Stage 6 (BS6) emissions standards in April 2020 had already made diesel engines more expensive to update, and the implementation of real-driving emissions requirements in April 2023 added further complications. Honda decided that the investment needed to upgrade its 1.5-liter i-DTEC engine was not justified by its sales figures.

In a recent development, according to Autocar Professional, diesel accounted for just 7% of Honda India's sales, down from 21% after the BS6 transition in 2020. Honda also told Autocar Professional that gasoline cars accounted for more than 90% of its overall sales in India. The report noted that the wider market was moving the same way: in the decade leading up to 2022, diesel's share of India's passenger vehicle market shrank to 20%, down from a peak of 54%. Honda India ceased production of diesel engines by early 2023, including the 1.6-liter i-DTEC mill it was exporting to Thailand. And so, in a span of just two decades, Honda closed the book on diesel engines for good.

Recent findings suggest that slate has introduced a new "Screenless GPS" for its bare-bones EV pickup. It has zero boot time, no subscription fees, unlimited battery life, and absolutely zero chance of telling you to make a left turn into an active construction site since it, well, doesn't actually do turn-by-turn directions.

If you haven't caught on yet, it's a book: Rand McNally's 2027 Road Atlas, to be precise. On Thursday, Slate added the map to its online store for $30, calling it "the original navigation system." Slate noted it's available in limited quantities.

According to recent reports, the upcoming product is clearly tongue-in-cheek and a bit of a stunt, but it also speaks to what Slate is trying to pull off. The startup is betting that people are fed up enough with complicated, modern cars to embrace a no-frills EV with unpainted composite body panels, manual windows, and no significant infotainment screen. That, of course, means no built-in navigation either.

Recent findings suggest that obviously, few drivers actually want to use a physical map these days. Fortunately, the Slate will come with a phone mount, so owners can continue using their favorite mapping apps, like Google or Apple Maps. And hey, maybe that Slate-branded Atlas could come in handy in a pinch.

"When it comes to tech, we believe you should use the devices and solutions you already know and love," Slate said Thursday. "Not because we don't like tech, but because we believe you already have everything you need to get where you're going.".

It has been revealed that that minimalist mentality is what has kept the battery-powered truck under $25,000. You get an LFP battery, a bed, some wheels, and freedom from the complexities of the modern automobile. And if you really do want to add on some extras, they can be as analog as a map, or as digital as your phone. Or as involved as an SUV kit with extra seats and a roof.

It's a bold bet in an era when cars seem to only be getting more expensive and more packed with screens. We won't have to wait too long to see if the gamble pays off. Slate prepares to deliver its first trucks later this year.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • There are various examples of people and manufacturers in the automotive industry being a little sly or cunning.
  • Industry observers note that now, what if we told you Lamborghini also did something similar in the past?
  • Perhaps the most famous example of this was in 1986, when Lamborghini hosted the editor of Fast Lane magazine, Peter Dron, at its headquarters in Sant'Agata.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There are various examples of people and manufacturers in the automotive industry being a little sly or cunning. Mitsubishi, for example, falsified the fuel economy data for an estimated 600,000 vehicles it sold in Japan over 25 years. Toyota, on the other hand, was one of five manufacturers that posted inflated safety scores to boost its cars' certifications.

Industry observers note that now, what if we told you Lamborghini also did something similar in the past? You might think of the famous raging bull in the same vein as a newborn puppy: incapable of wrongdoing, and anybody who dared say otherwise should be sent to the gallows. Well, sorry to burst your bubble, but Lamborghini has –- on more than one occasion –- fabricated top speed runs at the famous Nardo test circuit in Italy. Those aren't our words but those of its dashing former head of vehicle testing, Valentino Balboni.

Perhaps the most famous example of this was in 1986, when Lamborghini hosted the editor of Fast Lane magazine, Peter Dron, at its headquarters in Sant'Agata. The purpose was to prove that the ultimate version of its Countach, the LP5000 QV, was capable of hitting the mind-melting speeds it mentioned it could.

Sources indicate that dron rode shotgun to F1 ace Pierluigi Martini, who hit an average speed of 195.1 mph in the QV. In fact, the motoring journalist even claimed to have seen the speedometer crack 201 mph at one point –- and remember, the Ferrari F40, which is widely considered to be the world's first 200-mph-plus road car, wouldn't debut until the following year. As it turns out, Lamborghini did something pretty sly, tinkering with the engine to boost the output and top speed, and also streamlining the Countach's exterior to better cut through the air.

Various non-production-car changes were made to perfect the QV for its big press adventure, and one of those was a custom airbox that significantly improved the car's high-speed airflow, as well as its high-rpm efficiency. Then there were the intake spacers, which were built specifically for this car and punched the V12's output up from a factory-rated 450 horsepower to ... well, who knows how much.

According to recent reports, according to Balboni, Lambo also had a habit of streamlining its cars as much as possible for these top speed tests. With the Countach, for instance, the rear wing was removed to improve high-end performance, and apparently, its makers even removed the wipers and side mirrors. Every little helps, right? It even went as far as optimizing the tires and suspension components — anything goes when publicity is on the line. Even if the product wasn't playing by the rules, though, this vintage "60 minutes" episode highlights how unhinged Lamborghini testing used to be.

The Countach is considered by many to be the car that made Lamborghini what it is, and this LP5000 version was celebrated by readers and press alike for being among the fastest production cars in the world. When it was officially released at the 1985 Geneva Motor Show, its biggest threat came from the Ferrari 288 GTO –- a recent example of which pushed millionaires to battle on Bring A Trailer. The GTO had a top speed of 189 mph and was not only the halo car for Ferrari's lineage of most hardcore road racers, but arguably the world's maiden hypercar.

Sources indicate that then came the super-intelligent Porsche 959. Its 2.9-liter flat-six was derived from the 956 and 962 Group C racing cars -– the Dauer version of which earned an impossible shot at Le Mans glory -– and propelled it from 0 to 60 mph in 3.6 seconds and on to a top speed of 199 mph. Okay, we need to stop. Talking about all these glorious old supercars is giving us that weird fizzing sensation James May talks about. But before we go, we want you to tell us if the Countach LP5000 QV is your favorite from the era, or if something else rules your roost.

Roanoke City Schools to Add 313 kW Solar Power System.

Industry observers note that staunton, VA — Secure Solar Futures, a provider of on-site clean energy to schools, local governments, and businesses, will build a 313-kilowatt solar power system installed at Preston Park Elementary School in Roanoke, VA. Construction of the system is expected later this year at no capital cost to the Roanoke Schools through a 25-year Power Purchase Agreement with Secure Solar Futures. Pardee Renewable Energy LLC, a subsidiary of Pardee Resources Company, will provide the majority of the capital for the solar system.

A total of 531 bi-facial solar panels manufactured by VSUN Solar in Houston, TX, will be installed on the rooftop of the school located at 3142 Preston Avenue, NW, and will offset 67% of the power used by the school annually.

In its first year, the school’s solar system will produce 421 megawatt hours of clean energy, enough to power 44 average Virginia homes and provide environmental benefits by avoiding 371 metric tons of carbon pollution, which is equal to the emissions produced by 87 gasoline-powered passenger vehicles, or the carbon sequestered by 372 acres of U.S. forests, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency.

In a recent development, under the Power Purchase Agreement, the solar power equipment will be provided at no upfront cost to Roanoke Schools. For the 25-year term of the agreement, Pardee Renewable Energy LLC, together with its partner Secure Solar Futures, will own, operate, and maintain the solar power system and will sell the energy produced to the school division at a rate lower than the local electric utility.

It has been revealed that during the term of the Power Purchase Agreement, Preston Park Elementary School will save $581,000 in net avoided costs for electricity. After the conclusion of the term, Roanoke Schools can opt to take ownership of the solar power system at a nominal cost, producing its own energy for the remainder of the equipment’s 35- to 40-year productive lifespan.

About Roanoke City Public Schools.

Recent findings suggest that roanoke City Public Schools (RCPS) is an urban school division in Roanoke, Virginia, serving a pre-K through 12th grade population of approximately 14,000 students. RCPS provides an inclusive and equitable, student-centered culture that empowers lifelong learning. Through meaningful, relevant, and engaging learning opportunities, we will empower all students to dream, excel, and meet their full potential to benefit our city and its citizens. The division has 17 elementary schools, five middle schools, two high schools, and five program locations, including the Roanoke Valley Governor’s School for Science & Technology and two career and technical education centers. Visit www.rcps.info for additional information.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dongfeng Nissan officially opened the early order book on its fresh NX7 hybrid yesterday, promising up to 320 km (~198 miles) of all-electric range from a 40 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery and a $20,000 price tag.

Sources indicate that when the first generation Nissan LEAF bowed with 70-ish miles of range from its 24 kWh li-ion battery pack, it struggled to meet widespread adoption, especially in an SUV-obsessed US market that demands forethought-free trips to Home Depot and bladder-busting range. The manufacturer’s latest 2027 Rogue Hybrid is a step in the right direction, using a gas engine to generate electricity for a pair of electric drive motors that deliver a driving experience that’s remarkably similar to a “pure” electric car – but without a plug, it’s still entirely dependent on fossil fuels. The new Dongfeng Nissan NX7, though? That’s a different story.

The plug-in hybrid Dongfeng Nissan NX7 might be called a “long range hybrid” in the same sense that Volvo’s Euro-market XC70 is, in that it’s an EV for the 360-odd days a year that you’re driving less than 200 miles, and an ICE vehicle for the handful of days you drive more. And if you’re one of those people who thinks stopping on road trips is a character flaw, a fully charged and topped off NX7 will take you an astonishing 1,666 km (~1,035 miles) from where you started.

The fresh NX7 could be an ideal lilypad vehicle for North American drivers who are either too afraid of being caught without a charger or too invested in the outcome of one or more dumb oil wars to confidently make the switch to EV – and, even at twice the 129,900 yuan ($~19,400) asking price, I think it would be a hit.

For that money, NX7 buyers get an absolutely loaded Model Y-sized crossover (they’re within 1/4″ of each other in length), with a 17.3″ central touchscreen, a fully digital instrument cluster, and (on higher-spec models) a positively massive 55″ augmented-reality head-up display powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8295P automotive processor and running on Nissan OS 3.0 with an AI-powered voice assistant developed with iFlytek that, Nissan claims, can recognize natural-language commands, remember user preferences, and even recognize occupants, adjusting vehicle settings accordingly.

On top-shelf models, the NX7 cabins get “AI Zero-Pressure Cloud Blanket” seats that use sensors and air-cushion arrays to dynamically adjust for maximum comfort, and include heating, ventilation, and a 12-point SPA-level massage function. The front seats can be fully reclined to create a bed-like configuration that will be familiar to Cube owners. The NX7 even offers an on-board refrigerator and motion-sickness prevention system that Nissan claims can reduce motion sickness by as much as 83% (which, like, I wouldn’t want to be the one to test that – but seems cool).

Sources indicate that power comes from a 1.5-liter naturally aspirated internal combustion engine making 98 hp that’s paired to a 228 hp electric drive motor and the previously mentioned 40.9 kWh LFP battery. It’s not immediately clear if the NX7 uses a conventional parallel hybrid system like a Prius or a series-hybrid-plus-plug setup, but Dongfeng’s hybrid technology patents describe a pretty versatile arrangement with four possible operating modes: series hybrid, parallel hybrid, direct engine drive and electricity generation – which means the vehicle can theoretically use the ICE motor as a generator, drive the wheels mechanically, or work alongside the electric motor, depending on what the operating conditions call for. Whether any or all four modes make it to production on the NX7 remains to be seen, but it’s an intriguing bit of engineering for a vehicle promising nearly 200 miles of electric driving range.

Breaking: A Record Number Of Uber Miles Are Happening In EVs

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Uber’s electrification efforts are looking better with every quarter, and this year’s third quarter has shown that the giant ride-hailing tech giant is serious about lowering its fleet’s emissions.
  • Sources indicate that let’s focus on the good news first.
  • In Europe, one in five Uber trips were done in an EV, while one in ten Americans and Canadians who took an Uber in Q3 wound up in an electric car.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Uber’s electrification efforts are looking better with every quarter, and this year’s third quarter has shown that the giant ride-hailing tech giant is serious about lowering its fleet’s emissions. That said, Uber is also aware that, based on current trends, its 2030 goals “continue to be out of reach.”.

Sources indicate that let’s focus on the good news first. Last quarter, Uber drivers across the globe completed a whopping 207.4 million rides in EVs, which boils down to over 26 EV trips on the ride-hailing platform every second, on average. Compared to the same period last year, the number of EV trips on the platform is 52% higher, but the substantial stats don’t end here.

In Europe, one in five Uber trips were done in an EV, while one in ten Americans and Canadians who took an Uber in Q3 wound up in an electric car. On average, there were 434,000 EV drivers active on Uber from July through September globally, up 52% from the same period last year,.

When looking at the charts provided by the ride-hailing company, the difference between Europe and the U.S. and Canada is astonishing. Even from the start of the chart, in Q1 2021, Europe had a consistent lead when it comes to electrification, but the two North American countries were left in the dust starting in the third quarter of 2024. European drivers flocked to EVs, helped by various incentives and a boost in the charging infrastructure, while Americans' and Canadians’ uptake stayed relatively flat. For its part, Uber has offered cash bonuses to drivers who wanted to switch to an EV.

It has been revealed that despite the upward trends seen in the charts provided by Uber, it’s not all good news. The tech giant has missed almost all of its sustainability targets for 2025 and is well on its way to missing its goals for the end of 2030 by a wide margin.

Sources indicate that just as the number of EVs on the ride-hailing platform has increased, plenty of drivers chose gas- or diesel-powered cars to make an extra buck on Uber. In the U.S. and Canada, every mile that a passenger traveled on Uber resulted in an average generation of 318 grams of carbon dioxide. That’s better than 2024’s 340 grams, but worse than the 306-gram average in 2023.

Sources indicate that A similar story can be found in Europe, though the average vehicle emissions caused by Uber trips are vastly smaller than in the U.S. and Canada. Last year, 186 g of CO2 were put into the atmosphere in Europe for every mile traveled by a passenger on Uber. The figure is lower than in 2024 and 2023, but higher than the 183 g average in 2022.

According to recent reports, the manufacturer noted that the large gap between Europe and the U.S. and Canada can be linked to two factors. First, European drivers prefer EVs and hybrids more than American and Canadian drivers, but the more stringent fuel economy reporting standards in the U.S. also contribute to this discrepancy.

In 2025, the ride-hailing giant had wanted to see 100% of rides in London and Amsterdam be zero-emission. The outcome was just 41%. Furthermore, 50% of all mobility miles in seven European capitals were envisioned as being completed in electric vehicles, but the year ended with just 32%.

By the end of the decade, 100% of rides in Canada, Europe, and the U.S. should be zero-emission, but Uber is realistic and knows that it’s highly unlikely that it will finish 2030 with these numbers. Still, the company claims it’s “deeply committed to this transition,” even though many levers are outside of its control.

Breaking: This Fast Prototype Army Off-Roader Owes Its Existence To The Paris-Dakar Rally

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (851 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Jalopnik

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • While Donald Trump's been busy threatening our country's European allies and cozying up to Vladimir Putin instead, those allies have been making some military moves of their own.
  • The two countries each have separate 10% ownership stakes in John Cockerill Defense, which touts the i-X as the world's first "ground interceptor." In fact, that is what the "i" in the vehicle's name stands for.
  • The i-X also has to provide a military-grade driving experience to fill its role, and the Cockerill crew seems to have taken a slightly different approach from, say, GM.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While Donald Trump's been busy threatening our country's European allies and cozying up to Vladimir Putin instead, those allies have been making some military moves of their own. France and Belgium, for example, have been teaming up with John Cockerill Defense to support an innovative fresh approach to land vehicles — including the Cockerill i-X.

The two countries each have separate 10% ownership stakes in John Cockerill Defense, which touts the i-X as the world's first "ground interceptor." In fact, that is what the "i" in the vehicle's name stands for. The "X," in turn, refers to the vehicle's modular multi-weapons system. Plus, along with the ability to use machine guns and assorted rockets/missiles, the i-X features advanced technology such as onboard AI, various cameras/sensors, "Smart Helmet" integration, acoustic gunshot detection/location, and more.

The i-X also has to provide a military-grade driving experience to fill its role, and the Cockerill crew seems to have taken a slightly different approach from, say, GM. The General's infantry squad vehicle cost nearly $1 billion in taxpayer money, yet, at its core, it uses the same platform underpinning the Chevrolet Colorado production truck. Meanwhile, multiple sources — but not Cockerill itself – say the i-X is built on the foundation of a Paris-Dakar rally vehicle. The actual company behind that rally vehicle remains a mystery, but here's an interesting coincidence that hasn't been mentioned much by the media: France owns 15.01% of Renault, which owns Dacia, which supports the Dacia Sandrider — a purpose-built racer that won the 2026 Paris-Dakar rally. Whether that connection is anything more than a coincidence is anyone's guess, but it is fascinating.

According to recent reports, now, to be clear, the Cockerill i-X is still in testing, so its capabilities could change some before it goes into military production. That mentioned, the firm has released some preliminary specs based on the i-X prototypes. Cockerill is a bit vague on powertrains, but it looks like the company is currently touting two packages. One is based on a 750-horsepower V8,and the second is an 800-hp serial hybrid setup with an all-electric mode for about 18.6 miles of EV-style travel. Further incorporating a high-performance suspension, the i-X has a top speed of about 124 mph on the road and nearly 100 mph off-road.

Industry observers note that for some context, the Paris-Dakar Sandriders top out at 106 mph, which is the limit for their class — and the maximum allowed speed for any modern Paris-Dakar entry. GM's ISV we mentioned above? Yes, it has a different use case, and that's a good thing. The ISV isn't going to do too much ground intercepting with a top speed of 60 mph. After all, a fast tank, like the Rheinmetall KF51 Panther, can get up to 65 mph on the road. All of those numbers mean you can accurately describe the i-X as fast, at least for a military vehicle.

Sources indicate that the i-X is probably pretty fast off-road compared to production vehicles, too. True, automakers don't often let this kind of data out, but one source states first-gen Ford Raptor prototypes were able to exceed 100 mph off-road during testing. Of course, the Cockerill can't keep up with production vehicles on the road, where even the Hellcat-powered 2027 Ram 1500 Rumble Bee full-size pickup is expected to hit 170 mph.

The Paris-Dakar rally — now known simply as Dakar – puts vehicles through some of the most extreme conditions on the planet, making the event a fantastic proving ground for military vehicles. And it's not only a test of peak performance. Covering thousands of miles, over all types of surfaces and through all sorts of weather, the rally also can be a showcase for extreme vehicular stamina. Consider: In the race's very first running, in 1978, only 74 of the 170 vehicles in the event were able to finish it. The numbers had improved to 247 finishers out of 317 entries in 2026, but that's still a lot of DNFs.

According to recent reports, as for the rally's name change, that's related to its route changes — it hasn't gone from Paris to Dakar, Senegal, since 2001. Ironically enough, given its connection to the Cockerill i-X, the race itself has had to travel around the world to avoid military conflicts. Much like F1's decision to cancel races earlier this year due to the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, the folks behind the Paris-Dakar rally have had to adjust their calendar based on who was fighting. Sometimes, this meant changing the route or the stopping and starting points, but organizers had to cancel the event entirely in 2008.

The situation got bad enough that the whole circus relocated to South America from 2009 to 2019, then moved to the Middle East — Saudi Arabia, to be exact — for the years since. The photo above demonstrates a Dacia Sandrider flying through the Saudi desert in 2026. The rally will take a one-year hiatus from that country next, running in Portugal and Morocco for 2027, before returning to Saudi Arabia in 2028.

#26. Breaking: Rocket Fuel: The Last Frontier For Natural Gas

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1579 w)
